items.title: Another failed strategy?
items.description: PRESIDENT Donald Trump’s declaration of economic war on Iran is likely to backfire just like his bombing campaign failed to force Iran to surrender. It also exposed the limits of US military options. Wrapped in hyperbolic language, his threats to impose the “toughest sanctions in history” and “the most crushing economic operation ever taken against any country” were met with defiance by Tehran. Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi dismissed them, saying “We have seen this movie before”. Iranian officials warned of halting all oil flows from the Gulf and delivering an “earthquake-like” retaliation if Washington followed through. On what US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called Economic D-Day last week, he announced measures to sever Iran’s “financial lifelines” and force a “regime endgame”. But earlier, Trump telephoned Pakistan’s chief of defence forces, Field Marshal Asim Munir and asked him to persuade Iran to resume negotiations. FM Munir then headed to Tehran for talks with Iranian leaders. For all his blusterous rhetoric about “crippling Iran” the outreach was another sign of Trump’s desperation for a deal to end the six-month-old conflict. His flailing actions showed his growing frustration with a deeply unpopular war in his country. According to officials, Pakistan urged Trump to allow time for diplomacy to produce results. Even as mediation efforts got underway, the Trump administration went ahead with the announcement to ratchet up “unprecedented” pressure on Iran and compel it to return to the negotiating table. Iranian officials responded by saying they were “fully prepared” to counter the sanctions, which were an “act of state and economic terrorism”. Bessent widened the scope of economic sanctions against Iran but offered few details of what he called ‘Operation Economic Outcast’. Sanctions targeted Iran’s digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping sectors. It involved action against 60 entities, individuals and vessels. Alongside the financial measures Treasury Secretary Bessent warned the US would punish and isolate countries that continued to trade with Iran and had dealings with its financial system. His ‘either you are with us or against us’ mantra had a wearingly familiar ring. Trump had already issued the same ultimatum, threatening economic penalties against any country doing business with Iran. Tehran responded in kind. It warned that any state, including its neighbours, that joined US economic warfare would be treated as “an enemy”. Trump’s economic warfare will be as futile as his bombing campaign to force Iran to surrender. Bessent said Trump would be phoning some world leaders to ask them to cease their financial interactions with Tehran. But he named no target countries for secondary sanctions. Nor did he say what the penalties would be or specify any timeline for enforcement. No immediate action was taken against Iran’s biggest trading partners. That suggested that the door to de-escalation was being kept open. In any case, it was hardly the first time the tool of sanctions was deployed. Iran has been under multiple US sanctions for four decades and survived them. It seems ready to absorb the pain from this round too. It was also not the first time Trump targeted Iran’s trading partners. Before the war began, he announced tariffs on countries with business ties to Iran. The plan fizzled out and was soon overtaken by the US-Israeli military assault on Iran. For now, only the UAE has declared a halt to trade and financial transactions with Iran. This was before Bessent’s announcement and ostensibly in response to ballistic missiles being fired at it, which Iran denied. The suspension will add to Iran’s troubles with its fragile economy facing high inflation and a weakening currency. But it is unclear how and the extent to which the Emirati decision will be enforced. Qatar described US sanctions as unilateral and called instead for mediation efforts. The US depends on the cooperation of other nations to achieve the goals of its punitive economic campaign. China has already pushed back saying pressure tactics won’t work. After Bessent’s threat, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesman said China “will take all necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own interests” from “illegal unilateral sanctions”. Beijing warned of retaliation if the US imposes secondary sanctions. Washington is unlikely to go beyond threats and want a showdown with its biggest trading partner, especially with a Trump-President Xi Jinping summit coming up next month in Washington. Too much is at stake in that relationship to risk that. The US expectation that countries will fall in line assumes they will give preference to ingratiating themselves with Washington over their own economic interests. This will turn out to be another miscalculation. Many analysts also see it as unsustainable and resting on mistaken assumptions. As Robert Kagan writes in The Atlantic , “nations that depend on access to the strait — Japan and South Korea, for example — will have to choose between access to a reliable energy supply and participation in American-backed sanctions”. It is improbable they will choose solidarity with Trump’s Washington over their economic interests. He also points out that “the idea that, having survived both military strikes and sanctions, Iran will now succumb to sanctions alone is deluded”. At the same time, mediation efforts by Pakistan and Gulf countries are intensifying and making headway, according to credible reports. This suggests the warring sides haven’t given up on diplomacy. Behind the tough rhetoric of both countries, backchannel communication is aimed at getting negotiations restarted. Tehran wants the US to affirm and abide by the Memorandum of Understanding. Trump wants the Strait of Hormuz to reopen. Iran is reportedly preparing to submit its conditions for reopening the strategic waterway to mediators. The regional mediation initiative aims to first secure a ceasefire, followed by the prompt reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the termination of the US blockade. Whether this can be achieved in coming days remains to be seen. What seems clear is that Trump’s hope that America’s financial muscle will give him victory over Iran will prove to be as futile as his use of military might. The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN. Published in Dawn, August 31st, 2026

items.title: Gul Plaza fire commission blames no single entity or person directly
items.description: KARACHI: Deploring the failure to transform available resources into effective and coordinated firefighting and rescue efforts, the Gul Plaza Judicial Commission in its report says that the deadly inferno has signified a systemic failure across successive provincial and local governments as the legal and administrative mechanisms have existed, but could not be implemented effectively. The report of the commission, headed by Justice Agha Faisal of the Sindh High Court, was handed over to the provincial government months ago but authorities preferred not to make it public. However, the report, which bore no signatures, was silently released on Saturday apparently against the backdrop of the tragic incident at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims), Islamabad. In the report, Justice Agha Faisal notes that the tragic incident was a grave indictment of the failure of municipal and provincial systems to translate legal duties concerning urban safety into effective protection on the ground. In his report, Justice Agha Faisal says ‘sustained underperformance by public systems’ caused the tragedy; highlights failures of municipal and provincial systems It also states that the people have not only lost their lives to flames, but also due to delay, darkness, locked exits and windows of the ill-fated building, absence of fire safety systems, unimplemented audits/inspections and fragmented authority. The commission further says that Karachi Metropolitan Corporation, including its fire brigade, Sindh Building Control Authority, Rescue 1122, civil defence department, district administration and others bear institutional responsibilities for failure while material responsibility rested with the people acting as the de facto management of the building together with owners, occupants and commercial operators. It says holistically, the evidence suggested that the prevailing administrative and emergency response set-up did not appear to be adequately trained, coordinated or equipped to deal with an incident of such magnitude. Over 70 people had lost their lives in the devastating fire which had erupted on the night of Jan 17 and took nearly two days to be fully extinguished, leaving the ground-plus-three-storey building of Gul Plaza in ruins, with some of its sections collapsed. The Sindh government had constituted the judicial commission in February to investigate the deadly fire incident and to fix responsibility of any acts of commission or omission committed prior and subsequent to the incident. After conducting the probe, the commission had handed over the sealed inquiry report along with the entire record to the secretary law department in April. The 78-page inquiry report of the commission, issued by the home department, says that the systemic conclusion did not exonerate the institutions concerned nor did it single out the current period alone and instead the commission recognises that the tragedy was the human cost of sustained underperformance by public systems meant to protect life. “When a large commercial building remains unsafe despite known deficiencies, when audits do not result in compliance, when the building-control record is incomplete, when coordination structures remain on paper, and when rescue is attempted without fully exploiting available opportunities, the eventual loss is not merely accidental. It becomes the foreseeable product of systemic failure”, it adds. The commission’s report also states that the failure was not only limited to one department or building, but it was cumulative, layered and institutional as mechanisms, audit/building-control powers, firefighting obligations, emergency response structures and court-backed coordination framework had existed, but could not be implemented and the system did not function as a system. It further points out that the condition of the plaza, the opacity and incompleteness of its building-control history, absence of reliable inspection material at the stage of amnesty and regularisation, the persistence of audit non-compliance, the failure of coordinated enforcement and weakness of the emergency-support environment reflected a cumulative failure across successive provincial and local governments. “The commission does not make this observation to diffuse present responsibility. It makes it because the institutional truth of this case demands it. The risk at Gul Plaza accumulated over time because municipal and provincial structures, across successive periods, did not evolve or function in a manner commensurate with the hazards of dense commercial urban development”, it adds. The inquiry report says: “At the highest level, the case represents a systemic failure across successive provincial and local governments, in which legal and administrative mechanisms existed but were not effectively implemented.” The commission holds that the tragedy resulted from a convergence of known and unrectified hazards, inadequate managerial judgement, ineffective enforcement, fragmented institutional coordination, delayed and constrained emergency response and a system that failed to function as an effective whole. “The disaster was not merely the consequence of a fire. It was the consequence of a building left unsafe, warnings left unimplemented, authority left unexercised, and rescue opportunities left insufficiently exploited until irreversible loss followed”, it adds. It also says, “Therefore, those who perished in Gul Plaza Inferno were lost not only to flame. They were lost to delay, to darkness, to locked exits, to blocked windows, to absent systems, to unimplemented audits, to fragmented authority, and to a civic order that did not protect them in time. The present case is a grave indictment of the failure of municipal and provincial systems, over time, to translate legal duties concerning urban safety into effective protection on the ground”. Regarding the question of ignition, the material placed before the commission indicated a consistent and unrebutted position as the SSP (South) in his response confirmed the cause of fire because of children playing with and igniting matchsticks at shop No.193 in the plaza, and such fact has also been confirmed by an inquiry report of the commissioner of Karachi. Published in Dawn, August 31st, 2026

items.title: Eight killed and 18 missing after ferry capsizes off northern Cyprus
items.description: At least eight people have died, and 18 others are still missing after a passenger boat capsized off northern Cyprus, the head of the Turkish administration there has said. Ünal Üstel, prime minister of the self-proclaimed Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, said the ferry had been carrying 259 passengers and eight crew members when it began taking on water after departing the coastal town of Kyrenia on Sunday. The ship’s captain and seven crew members have been detained as part of an investigation into “how this tragedy occurred”, Üstel wrote on social media. Officials say the vast majority of those on board have been rescued. A search-and-rescue operation with Turkish authorities is underway. The boat has now sunk, and the authorities are attempting to recover its black box recorder to establish what happened. The privately owned ferry left the popular holiday resort of Kyrenia at about 12:30 local time (09:30 GMT). Üstel said the boat was scheduled to travel to Turkey on Saturday but was delayed due to poor weather. He told Turkish media outlet TRT that the boat was hit by two waves before it capsized. While the captain of the vessel was trying to recover from the first wave, a second wave hit and it began taking on water, he told the outlet. Rescue boats and helicopter around the sinking catamaran close to the port of Kyrenia Helicopters and coastguard boats have been dispatched to the scene, while ambulances have been stationed on the beach ready to receive rescued passengers. Üstel wrote on social media that the “priority right now is human life”, adding that security forces, rescue teams and health officials were all on the scene. He added the disaster will be thoroughly investigated and “even the slightest negligence will be uncovered”. “No one will be spared, regardless of who they are, who is found to be at fault or responsible,” Üstel said. Erhan Arikli, the transport minister of the self-declared Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC), which is only recognised by Turkey, told local media that 100 passengers had been taken to shore. Turkey’s President Recep Tayyip Erdogan sent his condolences to Turkish Cypriots and said efforts to reach those who were still missing “continue uninterrupted”. “Immediately after the accident, we launched extensive search-and-rescue operations in co-operation with the authorities of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus,” he said at a military ceremony on Sunday. Mustafa Koc saved around 65 people after his boat capsized. He told the BBC that he felt the crew should have waited until the sea was calm. “It wasn’t safe for them,” he said. “The sea was quite choppy.” Koc added: “People died. It’s not right.” He said the boat had arrived in Kyrenia on Saturday and “had some damage in the front”. Several rescue boats have been deployed by the coastguard to rescue passengers The ferry – a high-speed 40m long, 10m wide Filo Jet vessel – sails under the flag of Turkey, according to Marine Traffic. Filo Denizcilik, the company which operates the capsized passenger boat, said it was “deeply saddened by the tragic accident”. A hotline has been set up to provide passengers’ relatives with information. The nationalities of those who were aboard and the status of the injured are unclear. Local television has broadcast images of the upside-down ferry in the water, with people wearing life vests atop its hull. On Sunday evening, Arikli told TRT the ship had completely sunk. The TRNC, which is recognised only by Turkey, controls the northern third of the island of Cyprus, which has been divided since 1974. Additional reporting by Sherie Ryder

items.title: Filling in the connectivity puzzle
items.description: For all the progress Pakistan has made in expanding internet access, the coverage is still anything but reliable. Forget the mountains of Gilgit-Baltistan or the Thar desert; just try driving to the outskirts of a metropolis and see signal bars disappear on your phone. Ask any operator about it and they would, justifiably so, start a monologue about the underlying reasons. But with satellite, the whole connectivity landscape can change as billionaires (or trillionaires?) pour their money into expanding the technology. To understand whether they can truly scale, let’s first get a sense of how connected Pakistan is currently. By the end of FY26, the country had roughly 164 million broadband connections, of which an overwhelming majority — 159.5m — were via mobile data. Fixed makes up just 4.4m, roughly a tenth of all households. Within this smaller base, all focus lately has naturally been towards fibre, which has grown from around 100,000 connections in FY19 to 2.88m by June. While the rate of uptake is impressive, the sheer scale is still quite sobering, as under 8pc of households are fiberised. The problem is economics: laying fibre to a single home runs somewhere between Rs60,000 and Rs120,000, with most of the core inputs — the cable, optical network terminals, splitters — almost entirely imported, then hit with tariffs of around 70 per cent on top. The customer, though, pays only a small fraction, some Rs10,000-15,000 upfront. The internet service provider (ISP) must bear this capex, extending the payback period to eight or 10 years. The math only works where incomes and population density cross a certain threshold, which typically happens to be the same urban neighbourhoods already connected. In relatively remote geographies, mobile connectivity — let alone fixed — remains patchy still. For now, satellite broadband has limited ability to help bridge the connectivity gaps Since satellite terminals, by design, cater to a static location, they are sort of an alternative to fixed broadband. Both cater to non-individual use cases and usually offer higher speeds, and unlike fibre, this doesn’t require you to wait for an ISP to lay out a cable. While the technology continues to evolve, it faces two general constraints. First, satellite is slower than a wired connection — a matter of simple physics because the signal has further to travel — though in Pakistan you could well find fibre lagging behind not just satellite but even a good mobile connection. Secondly, in most markets it still costs more than what an average, or even well-off, household pays for a fixed line, even if that gap is narrowing. So where does it make the most sense to go for satellite instead? A few segments stand out. First are the connectivity deserts — Balochistan, upper Gilgit-Baltistan, the low-density districts where neither fibre nor a tower will make much sense — served either through Universal Service Fund subsidies or community leaders sharing a dish or two across a certain radius. Then come enterprise and continuity users, from remote offices still on VSAT (very small aperture terminal) links to premium urban households wanting a backup connection. There is also backhaul for remote towers: fewer than 18pc of Pakistan’s roughly 60,000 cellular sites are fiberised, a figure meant to reach just 35pc by 2032. And finally, the most niche of all, disaster response and mobility — floods, aviation, maritime — where the connection must survive an outage or travel with the user. Luckily, you don’t have to take my word for it, as we can learn from comparable markets that have already run the experiment. Nigeria is considered one of Starlink’s emerging-market successes, reaching around 92,000 customers by March 2026, with demand outpacing capacity in Lagos and Abuja to the point that signups were frozen and thousands pushed onto waitlists. Bangladesh sits in the opposite corner: nine months after launch, it had just 3,990 subscribers against a fixed-broadband base of roughly 14.5m, despite effectively rolling out a red carpet for satellite connectivity. That begs the question: what really predicts uptake of LEO (low Earth orbit)? We analysed a global panel, taking each technology as a share of households. Once you control for income, fibre and satellite tend to act as substitutes, though the effect holds only in poorer and middle-income countries and disappears among the rich. For incumbents, this poses interesting choices. Fixed-line ISPs face a possible substitution effect at the top end, since Pakistan ranks 143rd out of 149 countries on median fixed broadband speed, at a dismal 18.21 Mbps (megabits per second), compared with 125.59 Mbps globally. There is surely a segment tired of what it is currently getting, but how big is it? Under 4.7pc of all fixed connections have advertised speeds above 30 Mbps and not even 0.5pc above 100 Mbps — roughly 215,000 connections, under 5pc of the fixed base. Not much of a market, and urban density would complicate even that. Mobile operators, by contrast, might not face a serious direct threat, since the two go for different use cases. The real squeeze could fall on the GEO (geostationary Earth orbit)/VSAT layer, the PTCL Skylinks and Supernets, which serve exactly the enterprise, remote-site and continuity accounts satellite is built to take. To be fair, it was never a mass-market play to begin with. For now, the case for satellite rests on the state of technology as of today. But satellite is moving fast: launch costs keep falling, each new constellation adds capacity, and competitors like Kuiper are only starting to come online. None of that changes the basic logic, which is that satellite is a complement rather than a replacement. What it does change is the size of that complement, which is likely to grow. The question for Pakistan isn’t if there are large, even if not truly mass, use cases for satellite. It’s whether the regulation, the infrastructure and the pricing move fast enough to let it. Abdul Aziz Malik is an ex analyst at Data Darbar and Mutaher Khan is co-founder of Data Darbar Published in Dawn, The Business and Finance Weekly, August 31st, 2026

items.title: Jeux méditerranéens: Les Marocains Alami Laroussi et El Jardi décrochent le bronze au tennis double mixte
items.description: Le duo marocain composé de Younès Alami Laroussi et Diaa El Jardi a remporté, dimanche, la médaille de bronze du double mixte de tennis, dans le cadre des compétitions des Jeux méditerranéens, qui se tiennent à Tarente, en Italie. La paire marocaine s’est imposée dans le match pour la troisième place face au duo portugais composé de Francisco Rocha et Madalena Matias, au terme d’une rencontre disputée, remportée sur le score de 6-7 (4), 7-5 et 10-7. Younès Alami Laroussi et Diaa El Jardi avaient atteint les demi-finales après un parcours convaincant dans cette épreuve. En demi-finale, le duo marocain s’était incliné face à la paire espagnole composée de Lucía Cortez Llorca et Alejo Sánchez Quílez, au terme d’un match serré conclu sur le score de 6-3, 5-7 et 10-8. items.title: Six months on
items.description: IT has been six months since the US and Israel launched their war on Iran — a costly misadventure that remains far from being resolved. In fact, the threat of renewed hostilities is ever-present, despite efforts by regional states, such as Pakistan , Oman and Qatar , to revive peace talks. The war has been a miscalculation of Trumpian proportions, and the US president and his coterie of war hawks have few ‘good’ options to save face and bring their troops home. Despite the decimation of its religious, political and military top tier in the first few days of the conflict, Iran — which is militarily no match for the US war machine — managed to defend itself, and now conservative factions within the Iranian establishment are unwilling to back down. Rather, they seem prepared to absorb the pain and play the long game with the Americans. Yet instead of realising that the kinetic option has failed against Tehran, the US has stepped up its economic war against the Islamic Republic, warning sovereign states not to do business with Iran. While this action will impact the Iranian economy — which has survived sanctions for over four decades — it is unlikely to make Tehran raise the white flag, with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying, “pressure doesn’t work”. Moreover, China, the world’s second biggest economy and a major trading partner of Iran, is not buying it . As the Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said, Beijing “opposes illegal, unilateral sanctions”. Just as the US failed to defeat Iran on the battlefield, it may also fail on the economic front. Wise nations learn from mistakes. But while wisdom may admittedly be in short supply in the White House at the moment, it is time the US put aside its ego and committed itself to finding a diplomatic solution with Iran. The nuclear issue consists of hype more than any credible Iranian threat, while the Strait of Hormuz blockade by Iran is a direct result of the US aggression, with Tehran using the key waterway as a bargaining chip to secure its interests and security. The Islamabad MoU continues to offer the best available off-ramp to all sides, and both Washington and Tehran should return to the spirit of this document. The Iranian president has reaffirmed his country’s belief in dialogue; it is time President Donald Trump did the same. Instead of playing global policeman, the US should re-evaluate its role in the Middle East. Let regional states — specifically Iran and the Arabs — reach a mutually acceptable security framework. If there is to be long-term peace in the region, the US and Israel must end their armed aggression against sovereign states, and allow the people of the region to work out solutions amongst themselves. Published in Dawn, August 31st, 2026

items.title: Iran vows ‘decisive response’ to first US strikes in weeks
items.description: Iran and the US have traded fire after American forces struck two launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz, according to a US official. The first known US strikes on Iran since late July killed two people and injured two others, according to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), which vowed “response and punishment”. US Central Command said its forces had taken “limited, precise action” against “minelaying forces posing an imminent threat in the Strait of Hormuz”. Iran responded by attacking US military bases in Jordan, according to state media. Jordan’s army said it had intercepted eight missiles early on Monday morning. The US strike is the first known attack on Iran since President Donald Trump paused a renewed military campaign in late July. Larak Island is just offshore from the key port of Bandar Abbas and sits right on the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for global shipping. Iran is currently making tanker traffic pass by this island for checking and reportedly forcing vessels to pay $2m (£1.5m) to cross. Hossein Mohebbi, the IRGC’s spokesman, called the attack a “strategic and fatal mistake by the Trump regime” and said that the “enemy will pay the consequences of this miscalculation in both the economic and military fields”. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said in a statement quoted by state TV: “We are not seeking war, but we will deliver a decisive response to the aggressors,” according to AFP. Iran’s Tasnim news agency, which is affiliated with the IRGC, said earlier that the attack was carried out by drones. Hours later, Iranian media carried a statement by the IRGC saying it had attacked the US bases of King Hussein and al-Azraq in Jordan with ballistic missiles in response to the Larak Island attack. The IRGC said it had caused “heavy damage” and targeted “technical infrastructure, maintenance facilities, and enemy fighter jet positions”, according to a translation from the AFP news agency. Hours after the strike, Trump posted apparent AI videos on Truth Social showing oil infrastructure exploding. One was captioned “Kharg Island being blown to smithereens!!!” in reference to a major oil terminal off the coast of Iran which Trump has threatened to take. His post did not elaborate. Trump ​said last week that all mines‌ placed in the Strait of Hormuz by Iran as part of its efforts to blockade the route had been detonated or removed. He said Iran had been warned that any ship ​or boat deploying new mines would be ​destroyed. Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi described Trump’s claim as a “propaganda” deception. Iran is facing renewed economic pressure after Washington announced a fresh sanctions campaign on 24 August aimed at further isolating Tehran and expanding secondary sanctions against its allies . Iranian officials and state media have largely dismissed the campaign as a continuation of previous US economic measures, which they argue followed Washington’s military failure in the recent conflict. The US and Israel launched wide-ranging strikes on Iran on 28 February, with Iran responding by attacking Israel, US bases and allied states in the Gulf, and effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz to marine traffic. The Iran war has now crossed its six-month mark. Some 20% of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas used to travel through it before the war began.

items.title: Punjab moves to prevent Pims-like tragedies
items.description: • Orders Rescue 1122 deployment at all teaching hospitals across the province • 11-member working group to prepare SOPs for nursery, neonatology units LAHORE: The Punjab government has initiated multiple major steps at public-sector hospitals across the province to prevent a recurrence of the incident that clai­med the lives of 14 infants at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims) in Islamabad. The Specialised Healthcare & Medical Education Department on Sunday asked Emergency Services Department (ESD) Pu­n­­jab Secretary Rizwan Naseer to dep­loy Rescue 1122 officials at all government teaching hospitals across the province. Through an official letter, the health secretary apprised the ESD head that it had been decided to engage the services of Punjab Emergency Service Rescue 1122 to establish a uniform and standard emergency response mechanism and strengthen emergency preparedness, response and coordination at tertiary-care hospitals across Punjab. He said the main objective of the initiative was to establish a robust, integrated and uniform emergency response system with clearly defined roles, a command structure and escalation mechanisms across all tertiary-care hospitals. “Emergency officers will be responsible for standardising and monitoring emergency response protocols,” the letter stated, adding that the officers would coordinate with hospital emergency, security, fire-safety and other relevant teams. They would also be responsible for conducting regular inspections of emergency exits, fire extinguishers and life-safety arrangements. The health secretary also sought the names, designations and contact details of the officers to be app­ointed at the hospitals to discharge the assigned responsibilities. Technical Working Group Separately, the Punjab government has constituted an 11-member Technical Working Group (TWG), comprising senior medical teachers and doctors, to review and prepare Standard Operating Proce­dures (SOPs) for nursery and neonatology setups at all public-sector teaching hospitals in the province. A notification in this regard was issued, appointing University of Child Health Sciences Lahore Vice Chancellor Prof Masood Sadiq as its convener. According to its terms of reference, the committee shall develop clinical admission and discharge criteria to optimise utilisation and load management; establish formal step-down and shared-care pathways with peripheral hospitals to divert stable neonates for efficient utilisation of available resources; and guide hospitals on infrastructure requirements relating to fire hazards, electrical-load risks and evacuation challenges. Similarly, the committee shall draft comprehensive SOPs for fire safety, evacuation, firefighting and electrical-load management tailored to neonatal settings; design training modules for doctors, nurses and support staff on evacuation drills, neonatal handling and basic firefighting; and develop checklists and audit tools for regular compliance monitoring. The committee has been directed to submit its recommendations to the competent authority within seven days. Published in Dawn, August 31st, 2026

items.title: Barcelona close to deal for Arsenal’s Jesus
items.description: Barcelona are closing in on a move for Arsenal striker Gabriel Jesus worth £8.6m (10m euros). A deal for the Brazil international is believed to be at an advanced stage and, while the finer details still require finalising, the transfer is expected to be completed before Tuesday’s deadline. Napoli had shown an interest in Jesus, but the 29-year-old is set to join last season’s Spanish league champions and will travel for a medical on Monday. Jesus joined Arsenal from Manchester City in 2022, scoring 32 goals and adding 22 assists in 123 appearances for the Gunners. Speaking to the media on Thursday, Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta confirmed that Jesus was not training with the squad before Monday’s Premier League game against Aston Villa (20:00 BST). When asked whether that meant Jesus was leaving, Arteta said: “Personal situations, whatever they are, I think it’s clear.” Jesus would be Barcelona’s third signing from a Premier League club this summer, following the arrivals of Anthony Gordon from Newcastle and Rodri from Manchester City . Earlier this week, Barcelona’s pursuit of Atletico Madrid striker Julian Alvarez – also an Arsenal target – appeared to end as sources told BBC Sport that Atletico would not negotiate with their Spanish rivals. Meanwhile, Arsenal winger Gabriel Martinelli is set to travel to Saudi Arabia on Tuesday for a medical with Al-Hilal. It is believed a deal of at least £50m has been agreed for the 25-year-old Brazil international, after Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta made clear he is not in his plans. It is understood that Martinelli will sign a four-year contract, with Al-Hilal offering wages thought to be significantly higher than his reported £ 180,000-per-week deal at Arsenal . Analysis: Could Jesus’ injury history be a problem? By Elizabeth Conway , Spanish football reporter It looked as though Barcelona were not planning to sign another striker in the event of failing to capture Julian Alvarez from Atletico Madrid, who continue to make a deal extremely difficult. However, the unexpected availability of Gabriel Jesus has changed Barca’s approach. The Brazilian was not initially part of the club’s plans, but the circumstances surrounding his situation at Arsenal have opened the door to a move. Barcelona have taken advantage of the fact that he is no longer as prominent in Arsenal ‘s squad as he has been, especially with Kai Havertz and Viktor Gyokeres now ahead of him in the pecking order. With Jesus’ Arsenal contract running until the summer of 2027, the club are willing to consider his departure for a fee rather than losing him on a free transfer next year. The main question surrounding the move to Barca is Jesus’ injury history. He has suffered significant knee problems during his time at Arsenal . An anterior cruciate ligament injury to his left knee, suffered in January 2025, kept him out for 10 months. None of these necessarily means Barcelona will abandon their long-term interest in Alvarez. Following Robert Lewandowski and Ferran Torres’ departures from the club, Barcelona wanted to add a natural centre-forward to their attacking options. Jesus offers something different from a traditional number nine, with his ability to operate across the front line and contribute to the build-up making him an attractive option for Hansi Flick. If the deal is completed, Flick will be adding a highly experienced forward to his squad. Jesus made 27 appearances for Arsenal last season in all competitions, scoring six goals, while his six-season spell at Manchester City produced 236 appearances and 95 goals. For Barca, the move represents a relatively low-cost opportunity to add experience, versatility and Premier League pedigree to their attack.

items.title: Nasa launches new telescope to map cosmos
items.description: SPACEX launches Roman on a Falcon Heavy rocket from Nasa’s Kennedy Space Centre in Florida.—X/SpaceX • Roman designed to shed light on ‘unsolved mysteries’ including dark matter and dark energy • Also aims to discover thousands of exoplanets and supernovae • With its infrared vision, telescope will be able to detect light emitted by celestial objects billions of years ago WASHINGTON: Nasa laun­ched its new flagship space telescope on Sunday, embarking on a multi-year mission to create an unprecedented map of the cosmos and shed light on some of the biggest mysteries in physics. Designed to take a panoramic view of the vast reaches of space, the Roman Space Telescope “will help unlock the secrets of the universe”, US President Donald Trump said on Friday during a ceremony at Nasa headquarters in Houston, Texas. Standing over 12 metres (39 feet) tall, the state-of-the-art observatory launched from the Kennedy Space Centre in Florida aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket. Developed over more than a decade at a cost topping $4 billion, the telescope is named after pioneering US astronomer Nancy Grace Roman, who became known as the “Mother of Hubble”, another of Nasa’s flagship telescopes. While Hubble revealed that the universe is expanding faster than previously thought, Roman will seek to answer some of the other unsolved mysteries, including those of dark matter and dark energy. “Roman will give the Earth a new atlas of the universe,” Nasa administrator Jared Isaacman said in April when he unveiled the project to the press. Studying the invisible With a field of view more than 100 times larger than Hubble’s — and significantly wider than James Webb’s — Roman will survey vast swaths of the sky from a vantage point 1.5 million kilometres (930,000 miles) from Earth, which it will take about 100 days to reach. Designed to work in tandem with other observatories such as Webb, which offers greater power and precision, Roman aims to discover thousands of exoplanets as well as tens of thousands of supernovae, the explosive deaths of massive stars. “It will be the biggest catalog of astronomical objects anybody’s ever produced, and it will help us understand how common are solar systems like our own,” Dave Content, Roman’s technical manager, told AFP. The new telescope will also shed light on two of the biggest mysteries in physics: dark matter and dark energy. Their origins remain unknown, but together they are believed to make up about 95 per cent of the universe. Dark matter is thought to act as a kind of gravitational glue, while dark energy is believed to be a repulsive force driving the universe’s expansion. With its infrared vision, Roman will be able to detect light emitted by celestial objects billions of years ago, effectively looking back in time and offering scientists a glimpse into the universe’s distant past and helping them better understand these two mysterious phenomena. Roman’s observations will complement the work of the Rubin Observatory in Chile and the European Space Agency’s Euclid probe, and are highly anticipated because they could challenge scientists’ understanding of the universe’s structure. Published in Dawn, August 31st, 2026

items.title: Three-week international break a concern – Mourinho
items.description: Real Madrid manager Jose Mourinho has raised concerns about the impact of September’s three-week international break, highlighting how much time his players will be away from the club. “The international break does concern me,” Mourinho said. “It’s a lot of time.” Speaking before Sunday’s home La Liga match against Malaga (16:00 BST), Mourinho said he was mostly troubled by players linking up with their nations who then do not get game time. “Players who will join their national teams to play don’t worry me as much. It’s the ones who join the national teams and are not really involved that concern me,” he said. “We’ll see how we can go about this and work with the rest of the players. But not having players at my disposal for three weeks is a difficult situation.” The first international break of the 2026-27 men’s football season next month will last a week longer than usual, with the traditional October break now scrapped. In recent years, Fifa has used five primary international breaks during the season, in March, June, September, October and November. But instead of separate breaks in September and October, there will now be a three-week gap for international fixtures across late September and early October, when countries will play four international matches instead of two. The existing international breaks in November, March and June will remain. A number of reasons are behind the change, including the 2026 World Cup final being played on 19 July, the latest date for a summer World Cup since 1966. Player welfare and travel considerations were also taken into account when the changes were made. “I totally respect the players’ decisions and I don’t want to dramatise too much, but very often they pick up injuries during those breaks and right after returning from an international break,” Mourinho explained. “So it does worry me, but this is the way these things are and we can’t do much about it.” The Portuguese has already spoken at length about the World Cup players in his Real Madrid squad, including Jude Bellingham, Marc Cucurella and Kylian Mbappe, who have had a demanding summer. He said the club are working to manage their workload to reduce the risk of injury. In his pre-match media conference, Mourinho was also full of praise for Bellingham, highlighting his importance to the team beyond his attacking contributions. “He is a unique kind of player, extremely important for the team,” said Mourinho. “His mental strength, tactical ability, the way he recovers the ball, the way he pressures, the way he plays up front. “We like talking about Kylian, Vini [Vinicius Jr] and Jude, but I’m really happy with all the players. “We have great, great players here.” ‘Ballon d’Or winner doesn’t have to have won World Cup’ Mourinho also gave his perspective on the Ballon d’Or debate, arguing that winning the Champions League or World Cup should not automatically make a player the favourite for the individual award. “It’s a very beautiful thing individually, and that enters into the individual history of a certain player,” Mourinho said. “I think it’s normal that there are a dozen players of a very high level, of which we have three or four. It is normal that it exists as an ambition.” Mourinho suggested the prize should be ultimately measured by a player’s lasting impact on the game. “For me, the Ballon d’Or has to be one of those players that when he finishes playing, we miss for eternity,” Mourinho said. “I miss Maradona, Ronaldinho, Ronaldo, Cristiano, Messi, Zizou, Lothar Matthaus – I miss these people. “You can’t give the Ballon d’Or to a player because he won the Champions League or because he won the World Cup. It doesn’t have to be from Paris Saint-Germain or the Spanish national team.”

items.title: Bellingham scores as Mourinho’s Real win again
items.description: England midfielder Jude Bellingham scored a stylish goal to help Real Madrid beat Malaga in La Liga as returning boss Jose Mourinho racked up a third win in a row. Bellingham, who scored seven goals in the summer’s World Cup as the Three Lions finished third, got the first of Sunday’s match and his second of the season in the 19th minute. It came in superb fashion as he collected the ball 35 yards out and quickly dribbled past three players before shooting past Malaga goalkeeper Alfonso Herrero. Bellingham was heavily involved in Real’s second goal seven minutes later as he headed at goal after Herrero parried a strike. The ball then bounced off the Malaga goalkeeper and over the line, with it credited as a Herrero own goal. Real made it 3-0 after only half an hour to kill the game as a contest. Trent Alexander-Arnold, left out of England’s World Cup squad, recorded the assist, with his cross from the right superbly volleyed in by Kylian Mbappe. Real added a classy fourth goal in stoppage time at the end of the match when a quick break led to Vinicius Jr pulling the ball back from the byeline, with Arda Guler tapping in from close range. After the match, Mourinho called Bellingham an “incredible player” and added: “He is very demanding of himself and he is also demanding of others. I didn’t want to see him defend almost like a second left-back.” On the connection between Bellingham, Vinicius Jr and Mbappe, Mourinho said: “Very, very good players want to play together always, because they have the same speed of thought, the same quality and they always have to be compatible. “It was said that I didn’t want the three, but what I say is that I always want the best. There is empathy and collective work. They are all very good.” Mourinho returned to the Real Madrid head coach job in the summer, after previously being in charge from 2010 to 2013, winning the Copa del Rey in 2010-11 and La Liga the following season. Real sit top of the table on nine points, although Barcelona will join them on that total on Monday if they win at home against Rayo Vallecano.

items.title: Central Development Working Party clears five projects worth over Rs60 billion
items.description: • Plans include Gwadar water scheme, Karachi neighbourhood project, Gilgit medical college, NDU campus and Orakzai road • Study on wastewater treatment in Gwadar ordered to prevent sewage from polluting sea ISLAMABAD: The Central Development Working Party (CDWP) has cleared five development projects involving an estimated cost of over Rs60 billion, including a multi-billion-rupee water supply project to provide water from Mirani Dam to Gwadar through a 125-kilometre pipeline. The CDWP meeting, presided over by Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal, approved three development projects with a combined estimated cost of Rs11.7bn. It recommended two other projects worth Rs48.545bn for approval by the Executive Com­mittee of the National Economic Council (Ecnec), including the procedural clearance of the Rs19.55bn Karachi Neighbourhood Impro­vement Project (KNIP), which is already nearing completion with a World Bank loan. Under the current financial rules approved by the National Economic Council (NEC), the CDWP is empowered to approve projects costing up to Rs7.5bn, while projects with higher estimated costs are approved by Ecnec on the recommendations of the CDWP after technical clearance. Based on a technical evaluation by the Planning Commission, the CDWP recommended reducing the estimated cost of the “Construction of Water Supply Scheme to Gwadar Town from Mirani Dam under Balochistan Socio-Economic Deve­lopment Projects Phase-III” by around 20 per cent to Rs23.82bn, against the Rs29bn proposed by the Balochistan government. The reduction would result in an estimated saving of Rs5.235bn without any change in the design or scope of the project. The Planning Commission rationalised the project cost by 20 per cent, exclusively under non-scheduled items, which account for approximately Rs23.4bn, or 86.7pc, of the base cost, by curtailing contractor overheads. It has, however, asked Ecnec to approve the project subject to satisfactory resolution of outstanding technical observations, particularly regarding demand figures, hydrology, confirmation of the water source, procurement strategy, land acquisition status, a self-sustainable operation and maintenance (O&M) strategy, and a realistic implementation plan. While reviewing the project, Minister Ahsan Iqbal directed the provincial government to initiate a study on wastewater treatment in Gwadar, observing that the city should not be allowed to become another Karachi, with sewage polluting the sea. He also allowed the project to proceed to the bidding stage to save time, but directed that the contract should not be awarded until the project receives approval from Ecnec. The CDWP also cleared the “Karachi Neighbourhood Impro­vement Project”, with a revised cost of Rs19.55bn, for approval by Ecnec. The project is proposed to be financed through foreign funding, including an $85 million (Rs16.7bn) World Bank loan and Rs2.8bn contributions from the Sindh government. While discussing the Karachi project, the CDWP constituted a committee comprising the Planning Commission’s member (Population), member (Infrastructure) and a representative of the Economic Affairs Division (EAD) to develop a comprehensive framework for effective monitoring, transparency and accountability of foreign-funded development projects. Of the three smaller projects, with a combined estimated cost of Rs11.714bn, the CDWP approved the establishment of a Medical and Nursing College at Gilgit at an estimated cost of Rs4.924bn. The CDWP also approved the establishment of a National Defence University (NDU) FCS Campus at Defence Complex Islamabad (DCI) at an estimated cost of Rs2.75bn. It also approved the “Construction of Road from Zera to Daboori, District Orakzai (53.4 km)” at a cost of Rs4.037bn. The minister directed that funds be released before the winter season to facilitate completion of the project, which has been lingering since 2016. Published in Dawn, August 31st, 2026

items.title: Health minister opposes ‘permanent’ staff in public sector hospitals
items.description: • Mustafa Kamal says not minister’s job to manage a hospital; says elected mayor or his team should be looking after Pims affairs • Suggests bringing in CEO from private sector; all hirings on contract, performance-basis • New Pims ED takes charge, vows to prioritise patient safety ISLAMABAD: Days after a tragic fire at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims) claimed the lives of 14 newborn babies, Health Minister Mustafa Kamal seemingly stirred another hornet’s nest by suggesting that there should be no permanent employees at government-run hospitals. “There should be no permanent government scale employees in hospitals, they should all be employed on contract basis, and a CEO should be brought in from the private sector to run things effectively,” Mr Kamal said during an interview with Geo News on Sunday night. Lamenting that permanent employees were extremely powerful and embroiled their departments in litigation if they were ever dismissed, Mr Kamal touted his idea as the only ‘permanent solution’ to the prevailing rot in the country’s healthcare system. “Whoever performs and works should remain, everyone else should be let got. A CEO should be brought in [from the private sector] who should have full hiring-and-firing authority. They should get their annual budget approved from us and then be responsible for managing their affairs and ensuring accountability,” he said. Mr Kamal also noted that the inquiry report into the deadly fire in the gynae ward had found that only 120 seconds, or two minutes, elapsed between the first spark and the fire engulfing the entire Mother and Child Health Centre. When asked about a fire that had broken out in a Pims nursing hostel around a month ago, the health minister said he had only learnt of the incident after last week’s tragedy. He explained that at the time, a bulb in the waiting room of the nurse’s hostel had short-circuited and fell onto a sofa, which caught fire. He maintained that this incident was not reported to the ministry at any level, nor was it a major incident of the kind that would have been reported by the media. However, he maintained that the previous executive director (ED) had internally formed a committee to conduct an inquiry and provide a way forward. The report of that committee, he said, was only submitted to the ED just a day prior to last week’s tragedy. Referring to reports that he had already offered his resignation to PM Shehbaz, but was asked to hold off until the investigation into the incident concluded, Mr Kamal said the ministerial slot did not hold any meaning for him. He recalled how he had taken responsibility on the floor of the National Assembly. “When I am offering myself up for accountability, then no one should be spared… even though I am not at fault in any of this, but I do take responsibility as the minister,” he said. When asked about criticism against him and calls for his resignation – especially from the PPP – Mr Kamal regretted how the party was trying to link this to the issue of new administrative units, at a time when such a tragedy had taken place. However, Mr Kamal insisted that what transpired actually supports his viewpoint on the issue of new provinces . “If Islamabad were a separate administrative unit, with elected officials and a mayor who was directly elected by the people, they should be the ones tasked with running this hospital,” he said. Maintaining that he had to focus on larger issues, such as the country’s health policy, Mr Kamal insisted: “It should not be a minister’s job to run a hospital; it should be under an elected mayor”. To a question, he said that the new ED — who is the CEO of the National Institute of Health, Islamabad, had been appointed on the recommendation of the inquiry committee. He regretted that many of the top officials at such institutions considered themselves ‘kings’, since they were assured of the fact that no outsider could be brought in to take their place. “The new ED has been appointed after relaxing the rules; in principle no one can be brought in from outside… now we need post-facto cabinet approval for [the new ED’s appointment]. New ED takes charge Earlier, speaking to reporters after taking charge on Sunday, new Pims ED Dr Muhammad Salman said that patient safety would be his top priority. After taking charge of his post, Dr Salman visited different departments at the hospital and inspected arrangements in place. He also called a meeting of the heads of different departments and discussed the prevailing situation with them. Talking to media persons, he said : “Although it is a challenging situation but as responsibility has been given to me, I will try to prove myself. We will implement the recommendations of the inquiry committee and priority will be to ensure patient safety. The short term objective is to ensure that such incidents would not be repeated in future,” he said. Dr Salman said that other hazards will also be looked at. “There is heavy patient load on the hospital so it will also be managed. Referral system will also be made stronger so that the patient management would improve,” he said. Published in Dawn, August 31st, 2026

items.title: Tech trouble leaves Chelsea game ref without comms
items.description: When referee Michael Oliver emerged for the second half at Stamford Bridge on Sunday, something important was missing – his communications pack. For 45 minutes as Chelsea beat Brighton 4-3, a set of Premier League officials had to work without radio sets for what may have been the first time in 20 years. The referee, his assistants, the fourth official and the video assistant referee (VAR) team at Stockley Park could not talk to each other. Referees were first fitted with a microphone and an earpiece at the start of the 1999-2000 season, and while this did not become permanent initially, an upgrade allowed for more sophisticated radio technology to be introduced from the 2006-07 campaign. There have been problems with the battery packs or the communication link in the past. We have seen games held up while a technician fiddles with the device strapped to the arm of the referee or his assistant. But this is the first time it was decided the situation was not salvageable, and the officials would have to do their job the old school way. BBC Sport understands the crowd noise was not filtering out on the system, meaning it was difficult for Oliver, assistants Stuart Burt and James Mainwaring, and fourth official Tom Bramall to hear what they were saying to each other. Usually the chanting, shouting and singing of fans is suppressed, enabling clear communication. With headsets ditched, another obvious problem was created: how could the VAR, Andrew Kitchen, do his job if he could not talk to Oliver? A referee being able to speak to the VAR and describe an incident – like a penalty or a red card – is a cornerstone of the protocol. Kitchen had to continue working via a back-up system using messages sent to the referee’s watch. He could also talk to Bramall using radio communication. It did mean the VAR had to work slightly differently, with checks based purely upon the video official’s own assessment – rather than having the referee’s view to take into account. In an era where referees are asked to carry more and more kit – including invisible spray and RefCam gear – it might have been a relief to go out on the pitch a little lighter. And perhaps Oliver and Co enjoyed rolling back the years to how their careers began in the grassroots game.

items.title: Wife of man who died after turbulence sues airline
items.description: A widow whose husband died after “severe turbulence” on a flight has begun legal action against the airline. Lawyers for Linda Kitchen, 74, from Thornbury near Bristol, who broke her back during the incident, said her husband, Geoff, 73, was “fatally injured” when the Singapore Airlines flight from London Heathrow suddenly dropped around 6,000 ft (1,828 metres). She has now begun proceedings at the High Court seeking damages from the airline to help her access specialist support for her back. The BBC has contacted the airline for comment. “When I got separated from Geoff, I knew he was in a bad way, but nothing prepared me for hearing he had died. It was absolutely devastating,” she said. Kitchen and her husband, described as her “soul mate”, were starting a six-week holiday to Singapore, Indonesia and Australia when the incident happened in May 2024. The turbulence hit over Myanmar, with the flight then diverted to Bangkok, in Thailand, for an emergency landing. “There had been some turbulence over Europe, and it had been shaky over the water, but it was around 10 hours into the flight when we encountered the main turbulence,” Kitchen said. “It was so severe; it felt like the aircraft was dropping. I noticed my Kindle and Geoff’s phone had fallen to the floor, and I thought the plane was going down.” As the aircraft plummeted, Kitchen said her husband fell on top of her, squashing her into the armrest. Eventually, others helped to move him and a doctor on board began CPR. Kitchen was taken to hospital while her husband was still on the plane. It was two days before she was told he had died. It is understood that Geoff suffered a heart attack after the plane suddenly dropped at high altitude. Oxygen masks were deployed in the cabin during the incident “I spent 10 days in hospital before I was airlifted back to Bristol. I was in so much pain that the journey was a blur. Once back in the UK, I remained in hospital for around a week and, following my discharge, required significant assistance at home,” Kitchen said. Anthe Korelidou, a specialist aviation lawyer who is representing Kitchen, said: “That Geoff was fatally injured and Linda suffered severe injuries vividly highlights the severity of what happened. “While it’s more than two years since Geoff’s death, Linda and the rest of her family continue to have a number of questions and concerns about what happened and if more could have been done to prevent their injuries. “All Linda wants is for the most thorough investigations to be conducted. The issuing of High Court proceedings is a major milestone in being able to provide Geoff’s loved ones with the answers they deserve.”

items.title: Russia says it helped to repel Niger attempted coup
items.description: Russia has said its forces helped to repel Saturday’s attempted coup in Niger. Explosions and gunfire rang out across capital, Niamey, early in the morning, including at a key military airbase and the presidential palace. Hours later, Niger’s authorities said the rebellion had been contained. Nigerien forces had repelled the attack “with the assistance of servicemen of the African Corps of the Russian Ministry of Defence”, the foreign ministry in Moscow said on Sunday. The ministry also said it would continue to support Niger in its fight against “extremists”, but that the situation was now under the control of the legitimate authorities headed by President [Gen Abdourahmane] Tiani”. Russia’s African Corps has become a key security partner for multiple military governments in the Sahel, who have been struggling to contain long-running jihadist insurgencies. The Alliance of Sahel States – composed of Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso – said the attempted coup was “a betrayal by a group of soldiers involved in an attempt at destabilisation”. The authorities have not said how many soldiers were involved in the attempted coup, nor how many casualties there were. Niger’s military ruler, Gen Tiani, who was sworn in as its president last year after he deposed its elected leader, has also not publicly addressed the incident. The nation’s state broadcaster showed footage of several alleged mutineers being arrested by the Presidential Guard. On Sunday, Niger Press Agency reported that commercial activity was returning to normal, with petrol stations, shops and other businesses reopening. Supporters of the government gathered at a public square in central Niamey in support of the security forces and Tiani’s government. Air Base 101, the military site attacked on Saturday, is part of the Diori Hamani airport complex. It hosts Nigerien military aircraft and drones, as well as an Alliance of Sahel States counter-terrorism unit. Russian and Italian forces are also based there, according to news agency Reuters. Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso are all military-ruled countries that have cut ties with Western partners and strengthened their co-operation with Russia. But jihadist violence remains widespread in all three countries, despite the shift in alliances. For Niger’s government, Saturday’s mutiny highlights that the military is dealing not only with an external insurgency, but also signs of discontent within its own ranks. The airbase where the mutiny began had itself been targeted twice by jihadists this year – once by an Islamic State affiliate and later by an al-Qaeda affiliate. Nigerien authorities say security forces have increased patrols around key sites in Niamey following the attempted takeover, including the main airport entrance and the presidential pavilion.

items.title: Réseaux électriques : un groupe chinois s’implante au Maroc
items.description: Nari Technology, spécialisé dans l’automatisation et les équipements pour réseaux électriques, vient d’entrer sur le marché marocain. Le groupe, contrôlé en dernier ressort par State Grid Corporation of China, a engagé ses premières activités dans le royaume au premier semestre 2026, alors que ses revenus à l’international ont presque triplé sur un an. Un nouvel acteur chinois des infrastructures électriques vient d’entrer sur le marché marocain. Nari Technology, spécialisé dans l’automatisation et les équipements pour réseaux électriques, a engagé ses premières activités dans le royaume au premier semestre 2026, selon son rapport semestriel publié récemment. Le groupe chinois cite le Maroc parmi les nouveaux marchés abordés durant les six premiers mois de l’année, aux côtés du Kirghizstan. Mais son rapport ne permet pas encore de mesurer précisément l’ampleur de cette arrivée. Nari ne précise ni la nature des équipements concernés, ni l’identité d’un éventuel client marocain, ni la valeur d’un contrat. Ses comptes ne détaillent pas non plus les revenus réalisés dans chaque pays à l’international. Le chiffre d’affaires éventuellement généré au Maroc ne peut donc pas être isolé. L’international prend de l’importance Cette arrivée intervient alors que Nari Technology accélère fortement son développement hors de Chine. Sur les six premiers mois de 2026, ses activités internationales ont généré 5,9 milliards de yuans, soit environ 8,1 milliards de dirhams. Sur un an, ces revenus ont bondi de 196,6 %. À l’inverse, le chiffre d’affaires réalisé en Chine a reculé de 1,9 %, à 21,8 milliards de yuans, l’équivalent d’environ 30 milliards de dirhams. À l’échelle du groupe, le chiffre d’affaires semestriel s’est établi à 27,8 milliards de yuans, soit quelque 38,3 milliards de dirhams, en progression de 14,5 %. Le bénéfice net attribuable aux actionnaires a atteint 3,07 milliards de yuans, environ 4,2 milliards de dirhams, en hausse de 4,1 %. Des technologies au cœur des nouveaux réseaux électriques Nari Technology intervient sur un marché directement lié à la transformation des systèmes électriques. Le groupe développe notamment des systèmes de conduite et de protection des réseaux, des équipements d’électronique de puissance, des solutions de stockage d’électricité et des technologies destinées à faciliter l’intégration des énergies renouvelables. Les équipements liés aux réseaux électriques intelligents constituent son principal pôle d’activité. Ils ont généré 13,3 milliards de yuans de revenus au premier semestre, soit environ 18,3 milliards de dirhams. Les activités liées à l’énergie bas carbone ont, pour leur part, atteint 9,6 milliards de yuans, près de 13,2 milliards de dirhams, en progression de 47 % sur un an. Les solutions combinant numérique et énergie ont généré 3,7 milliards de yuans, soit environ 5,1 milliards de dirhams. Les systèmes industriels connectés ont rapporté 953,7 millions de yuans, près de 1,3 milliard de dirhams. Le groupe multiplie par ailleurs les projets à l’étranger. Il indique avoir introduit ses unités terminales distantes au Chili, ses compensateurs synchrones statiques en Arabie saoudite et aux Philippines, ainsi que ses systèmes d’automatisation de distribution au Pérou. En Australie, Nari fournit des équipements destinés à l’alimentation électrique ferroviaire. Le groupe fait également état à Oman d’un contrat clés en main portant sur une installation de stockage d’électricité d’une capacité de 500 MW et 2 000 MWh. Contrôlé en dernier ressort par State Grid Corporation of China, Nari Technology aborde ainsi le marché marocain avec une offre centrée sur des équipements et technologies liés à la modernisation des réseaux électriques. Les détails de ses premières opérations dans le royaume restent toutefois à préciser. The post Réseaux électriques : un groupe chinois s’implante au Maroc appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Wydad : les tensions autour de Ziyech s’intensifient avant le début de la saison
items.description: Des sources informées proches du Wydad Athletic Club ont révélé à « Hesport » les détails d’un différend survenu entre l’international marocain Hakim Ziyech et l’entraîneur portugais Paulo Sérgio lors du match amical disputé samedi dernier par le club casablancais face à la Renaissance de Zemamra, dans le cadre de la préparation de la saison sportive 2026-2027. Selon les mêmes sources, Ziyech devait participer à la seconde période de la rencontre. Il avait rejoint les vestiaires avec ses coéquipiers à la mi-temps, après avoir effectué des exercices d’échauffement avec plusieurs joueurs durant la première période en vue de son entrée en jeu. Cependant, alors qu’il se préparait à regagner la pelouse, le joueur aurait été informé par Paulo Sérgio qu’il ne participerait finalement pas à la seconde période. Il lui aurait également été indiqué qu’il ne ferait pas partie du groupe qui se rendra à Agadir pour le prochain stage de préparation. Les sources précisent que l’entraîneur portugais aurait expliqué à Ziyech que la décision de ne pas le faire jouer et de ne pas l’inclure dans le déplacement à Agadir résultait d’instructions de Brahim El Asri, président du club. Le joueur aurait alors directement contacté le président du Wydad afin de lui demander des explications sur cette décision. Toujours selon ces sources, El Asri aurait nié, lors de son échange avec Ziyech, avoir donné des instructions à l’entraîneur pour l’empêcher de jouer ou l’écarter du voyage à Agadir. La situation aurait ensuite dégénéré en différend entre le joueur et le technicien portugais, allant jusqu’à une altercation verbale entre les deux hommes. D’après les informations disponibles, l’incident aurait suscité la désapprobation de plusieurs joueurs du Wydad, qui auraient estimé que la manière dont la situation avait été gérée ne correspondait pas aux standards attendus au sein d’un club professionnel. Dans les heures qui ont suivi l’incident, Ziyech aurait fini par être convaincu que son exclusion du match et du déplacement à Agadir était effectivement liée au président du club. Il a alors choisi de répondre indirectement en commentant une publication sur une page de supporters du Wydad sur Instagram. Ziyech a écrit dans son commentaire : « Va demander à ton président pourquoi il a refusé de me laisser jouer le match et pourquoi il a refusé que je voyage à Agadir », ajoutant une remarque sarcastique laissant entendre que cette version pourrait être démentie par la suite. Ces développements interviennent alors que la direction du Wydad et Hakim Ziyech avaient déjà engagé des discussions sur une éventuelle révision de son salaire afin de l’adapter aux capacités financières actuelles du club, le joueur disposant de l’un des contrats les plus coûteux de l’effectif. La détérioration des relations entre Ziyech, d’une part, et la direction du Wydad ainsi que l’entraîneur Paulo Sérgio, d’autre part, pourrait accélérer le départ du joueur du club casablancais dans les prochaines semaines. Il reste toutefois à déterminer si la direction interviendra pour apaiser les tensions et rétablir le calme avant le début de la nouvelle saison. Selon les mêmes sources, l’incident a également suscité le mécontentement d’une partie des supporters du Wydad, qui ont dénoncé la manière dont le dossier d’un joueur jouissant d’une place particulière auprès du public a été géré. Certains estiment que la situation de Ziyech aurait nécessité davantage de souplesse afin d’éviter que le différend ne se transforme en crise susceptible d’affecter l’image et la stabilité du club avant le coup d’envoi de la nouvelle saison. « Hesport » a tenté de joindre Brahim El Asri, président du Wydad Athletic Club, afin de l’interroger sur les détails de l’incident et recueillir sa version des faits, mais son téléphone est resté sans réponse. items.title: Le Général Célestin Simporé en première ligne : « L’unité et la solidarité sont les clés de notre victoire »
items.description: Dans le cadre de la dynamique révolutionnaire et populaire portée par la Transition, une importante délégation gouvernementale s'est rendue sur le terrain ce samedi 29 août 2026. Conduite par le Ministre d’État en charge de la Guerre, le Général de division Célestin Simporé, et accompagnée du Président de la Commission nationale de la Confédération des États du Sahel (CN-CES), Bassolma Bazié, cette tournée de mobilisation a permis d'aller au contact direct des forces de défense et de sécurité (FDS) et des Volontaires pour la défense de la patrie (VDP). Des garnisons du Nord aux détachements de Koudougou et Ténado, les autorités ont martelé l'impératif d'unité et de cohésion pour vaincre le terrorisme et parachever la reconquête intégrale du territoire national. L'engagement pour la souveraineté et la libération totale du territoire burkinabè franchit une nouvelle étape de mobilisation sur le terrain. Ce samedi 29 août 2026, le Ministre d’État, Ministre de la Guerre et de la Défense patriotique, le Général de division Célestin Simporé, a pris la tête d'une tournée d'envergure menée dans la région du Nord ainsi que dans les zones de Koudougou et Ténado. Signe de la forte cohésion et de l'intégration des efforts au sein de l'alliance régionale, cette mission a vu la participation active du Président de la Commission nationale de la Confédération des États du Sahel (CN-CES), le camarade Bassolma Bazié. Ensemble, les deux responsables sont allés galvaniser les forces de défense et de sécurité (FDS) et les Volontaires pour la défense de la patrie (VDP) face aux défis sécuritaires contemporains. Cette sortie de terrain a constitué un moment privilégié d’échanges directs et sans intermédiaire avec les unités opérationnelles de première ligne. Les discussions ont tourné autour des grandes orientations stratégiques définies par le Président du Faso, le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, ainsi que de la dynamique globale de la Révolution progressiste et populaire actuellement en cours au Burkina Faso. Du prestigieux 3e Bataillon d’infanterie aéroporté (BIA) de Koudougou jusqu’au détachement militaire de Ténado, le Ministre d’État a inlassablement partagé un message de fermeté et d'espoir. Il a réaffirmé avec force que l’unité, la cohésion et la solidarité au sein de l’ensemble des forces armées constituent les clés de voûte de l'efficacité opérationnelle et la condition unique pour rétablir l'intégrité du territoire. Au-delà de la remobilisation tactique, cette tournée a également été l'occasion pour la hiérarchie de témoigner la reconnaissance de la Nation envers ses défenseurs. Le Général Simporé a chaleureusement salué les efforts constants et les lourds sacrifices consentis quotidiennement par les forces combattantes sur le théâtre des opérations. Tout en se félicitant des résultats concrets et encourageants déjà enregistrés dans la neutralisation des groupes terroristes, le Ministre a solennellement appelé les hommes à maintenir et à renforcer l’effort collectif. Face à un ennemi asymétrique, la Transition burkinabè démontre que la réponse nationale repose plus que jamais sur la cohésion absolue entre ses forces régulières, ses volontaires civils et ses institutions de souveraineté. items.title: Scandale foncier à Bobo-Dioulasso : L’ex-ministre Lionel Bilgo placé sous mandat de dépôt
items.description: L’ancien ministre de l’Éducation nationale et porte-parole du gouvernement de Transition, Lionel Wendkouni Joël Bilgo, ainsi que son directeur exécutif, Vincent de Paul Kaboré, ont été placés sous mandat de dépôt ce vendredi 28 août 2026. Poursuivis par le parquet de Bobo-Dioulasso pour exercice illégal d’activités de promotion foncière et de publicité sans autorisation préalable au sein de la société immobilière SITRAF, ils risquent jusqu'à dix ans de prison et des amendes astronomiques. Ce coup de filet spectaculaire, mené sous la direction du Procureur du Faso Sékou Traoré, marque un tournant répressif majeur dans l'application de la nouvelle législation sur la promotion immobilière au Burkina Faso. L'annonce a fait l'effet d'une onde de choc dans les milieux politiques et économiques burkinabè. L'économiste, écrivain et ancien ministre de l'Éducation nationale sous la transition de Paul-Henri Sandaogo Damiba, Lionel Wendkouni Joël Bilgo, dort désormais en prison. Le gérant de la Société Immobilière TRAORE et FRERES (SITRAF) a été déféré et écroué le 28 août 2026 en compagnie de son directeur exécutif, Vincent de Paul Kaboré. Tous deux font face à la rigueur de la loi pénale après des révélations accablantes sur les activités commerciales de leur entreprise à Bobo-Dioulasso. L’affaire a démarré le 19 août 2026. Ce jour-là, le commissariat central de police de Bobo-Dioulasso est alerté des agissements de la société SITRAF, soupçonnée de vendre des parcelles nues et d'en faire la publicité sans aucune autorisation légale. Immédiatement saisi, le Procureur du Faso ordonne l'ouverture d'une enquête minutieuse. La perquisition effectuée au siège de l'entreprise permet aux enquêteurs de mettre la main sur des documents hautement compromettants, notamment des attestations d'attribution de parcelles. Les investigations révèlent également que la SITRAF s'était engagée dans des chantiers de construction sur trois sites distincts : deux à Léguéma, couvrant une superficie totale de 197 hectares, et un à Lôgôfourousso, d'une superficie de 16 hectares. Le piège du morcellement illégal de 213 hectares Lors de leurs interrogatoires, Lionel Bilgo et Vincent de Paul Kaboré ont reconnu que leur société disposait d'un agrément officiel (N°2026-003/MUH/CAB du 12 janvier 2026). Toutefois, ce document l'autorisait exclusivement à construire une cité sur chacun de ses trois sites. En aucun cas la SITRAF n'avait le droit de procéder au morcellement de ces terres aux fins de vente de parcelles nues, ni d'en faire la publicité. En agissant de la sorte, les dirigeants ont violé de manière caractérisée les dispositions des articles 2, 4 et 11 de la loi n°2023-008/ALT du 20 juin 2023 portant promotion immobilière au Burkina Faso. Plusieurs témoins ont d'ailleurs confirmé aux enquêteurs avoir déjà payé des parcelles nues auprès de la société, le nombre exact de lots vendus restant encore à déterminer. Face à la gravité des faits constatés, le parquet a décidé de poursuivre les dirigeants ainsi que la personne morale SITRAF pour exercice illégal d'activités de promotion foncière et de publicité sans autorisation préalable. Les prévenus risquent de lourdes sanctions : la loi prévoit des peines d’emprisonnement allant de six mois à dix ans, couplées à des amendes pouvant atteindre cent millions (100 000 000) de francs CFA à l'hectare de terrain aménagé, et jusqu'au double du montant des parcelles vendues. Dans son communiqué officiel, le Procureur du Faso, Sékou Traoré (Chevalier de l'Ordre du Mérite), a invité toutes les victimes potentielles à se faire connaître et a appelé la population burkinabè à faire preuve de la plus grande vigilance face aux offres foncières suspectes. Le face-à-face final avec les juges est désormais imminent : le dossier sera officiellement enrôlé à l’audience du vendredi 4 septembre 2026 pour y être jugé.
