Ioba / Dissihn : La semaine de la citoyenneté met l’accent sur la sécurité routière
items.description: Burkina-Ioba-Citoyenneté Ioba / Dissihn : La semaine de la citoyenneté met l’accent sur la sécurité routière Dissihn, 29 août 2026 (AIB) – Le président de la délégation spéciale (PDS) de la commune de Dissihn, Benjamin Nana, en collaboration avec l’Office national de la sécurité routière (ONASER), a procédé le jeudi 14 août 2026, au lancement officiel de la 14e édition de la Semaine de la citoyenneté, placée sous le thème : « Nous nous tuons sur la route ». Durant cinq jours, les activités prévues visent à sensibiliser les populations sur l’incivisme routier et à promouvoir l’adoption de comportements responsables afin de réduire les accidents de la circulation. La cérémonie de lancement, présidée par Évariste Méda, conseiller au secrétariat permanent de la magistrature, s’est déroulée en présence des autorités administratives, communales, des responsables de l’ONASER et d’une importante mobilisation de la population. Pour le promoteur de la manifestation, Honoré Somda, les accidents de la circulation ne doivent pas être considérés comme une fatalité. « Les accidents ne sont pas une question de fatalité, il faut un changement de comportement », a-t-il martelé, appelant à une implication accrue des autorités locales dans les actions de sensibilisation. « C’est pourquoi nous avons mis les autorités communales au-devant pour que la sensibilisation ait un impact réel sur le terrain », a-t-il ajouté. Le représentant du parrain, Firmin Hien, a salué la pertinence du thème, estimant que le message « Nous nous tuons sur la route » constitue une interpellation pour l’ensemble des burkinabè, particulièrement pour les populations de Dissihn. S’adressant à la jeunesse, il a appelé celle-ci à cultiver les vertus cardinales nécessaires au développement de la commune. Prenant la parole, le PDS de Dissihn, Benjamin Nana, a dressé un état des lieux de l’incivisme routier au Burkina Faso et dans sa commune. Il a invité les populations à saisir cette semaine comme une occasion de remise en question et de changement de comportement. Il a également appelé les habitants à participer massivement aux activités programmées afin de renforcer la citoyenneté et le vivre-ensemble. Selon le président du comité d’organisation, Jean-Luc Somé, plusieurs activités sont prévues au cours de la semaine. Il s’agit notamment de séances de sensibilisation sur la sécurité routière dans les principaux carrefours de la ville, de projections de films éducatifs, de jeux-concours et d’émissions radiophoniques interactives. À travers cette campagne, l’ONASER entend renforcer la prise de conscience des usagers de la route et contribuer à une réduction des comportements à risque dans la commune de Dissihn. Agence d’information du Burkina JBD/SZ-DNK

items.title: What to Read to Wake Up Your Brain
items.description: Summer is the ideal season for fun, frothy reads. On languorous weekends or hard-earned vacations, many people skew their literary diet toward lighter fare—fast-paced thrillers, steamy rom-coms—rather than, say, an in-depth history or an experimental novel. But fall is fast approaching. For some, that means a return to school; for many others, it represents the end of the most leisurely time of the year. Whether or not you’re heading back to the classroom, you may soon be tasked with, or else seek out, a more vigorous reading regimen; generally, the autumn months tend to require more from our brain. But it’s useful, as Labor Day approaches, to have an on-ramp—a way of easing into that more intense intellectual mode. These six books can help reacquaint the fall reader with the pleasures and demands of paying serious attention. Although none of them is especially strenuous—most are either brisk, bite-size, or divided into digestible parts—they are undeniably stimulating. Each will give your mind a much-needed burst of energy. The Age of Innocence , by Edith Wharton I came late to Wharton’s 1920 novel about a high-society love triangle in Gilded Age New York City—in fact, I read it only two months ago. I had gotten into my head that the writing would be too ornate for my liking, the settings and dialogue too stuffy. But classics tend to be classics for a reason, and The Age of Innocence snapped me out of my heat-induced inertia. Wharton’s witty, sophisticated sentences require and then amply reward sustained attention. Narrating the follies and frivolities of the city’s elite, she’s sarcastic and allusive, winking even as she dazzles with dialogue that verges on poetry. (The novelist Roxana Robinson once compared Wharton’s diction to a “sword wrapped in satin.”) Yet the universality of the novel makes it a perfect gateway for reengaging with foundational literature: Its core subjects are the timeless tensions between desire and obligation, and between self and society, expressed through a smoldering romance between forbidden lovers. Any Person Is the Only Self , by Elisa Gabbert One of the best entry points to rigorous reading is our own curiosity. Genuine interest is powerful; it can help readers move through the most daunting chapters or grasp even the most complicated ideas. As both a reader and a writer, Gabbert has always been guided by the compass of her inquisitiveness, perhaps never more so than in her wide-ranging third essay collection. The author’s sense of wonder stimulates the reader’s, and her primary subject—literature—may lead one to more invigorating reading. She is as erudite as she is earnest, and as she ponders Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein and Marcel Proust’s Swann’s Way , or the lives and work of Sylvia Plath and Rainier Maria Rilke, her passion becomes contagious. As she suggests in an essay about her classic-literature book club, it’s always worth finding time to have your own “intimate experience” with famous novels. Following the winding pathways of Gabbert’s mind might well show you to your next great read. [ Read: The end of reading is here ] Enough Is Enuf , by Gabe Henry Few books have made me laugh harder or more frequently than Henry’s exploration of the English language’s nonsensical writing system—one in which the spelling of words tells us precious little about how they’re pronounced—and the centuries of failed attempts to fix it. Enough Is Enuf chronicles some of the staunchest advocates of “simplified spelling” systems (including Teddy Roosevelt, Mark Twain, and the dictionary maker Noah Webster), each of whom attempted to streamline the haphazard rules of written English—a uniquely weird amalgamation of other, older languages. Henry’s book sits at the nexus of linguistics and history—two subjects that can be daunting, in many cases making for dry reading—but it is brisk and entertaining, full of archival images, clarifying examples, and hilarious anecdotes. By its end, you’ll likely feel grateful for the miracle that is your own literacy and eager to read more about quirky characters, both human and lexicographic. Suppose a Sentence , by Brian Dillon Each of the 27 short essays in this collection is inspired by a single sentence that captured Dillon’s imagination. For more than a quarter century, the critic has kept dozens of notebooks in which he copies down striking phrases he’s stumbled across. They vary widely in length, register, and complexity: the cascading clauses of Roland Barthes, a nine-word short-story opener by Susan Sontag, the prince of Denmark’s dying “O, o, o, o” in Hamlet . Each essay is a perfect introduction to its source material, providing both a hook (the sentence) and a primer (Dillon’s reflections) to an eclectic set of authors (who also include Gertrude Stein, James Baldwin, and Hilary Mantel). Dillon’s notebook exercise, I might add, could be just the thing to re-attune one’s brain to the wonders of the written word. [ Read: The adults who treat reading like homework ] Practice , by Rosalind Brown Brown’s trim novel takes place over a single day in the life of Annabel, an Oxford undergrad who’s trying to write an essay about Shakespeare’s sonnets. The paper’s due tomorrow, and it’s not going well: She’s constantly interrupted by roving, unruly thoughts and a very demanding body (she’s hungry, now she’s horny, and now she’s gotta pee). She’d planned to stick to a rigid routine—a 6 a.m. wake-up, a distraction-free morning of work, a break to walk through campus—but is consistently derailed. (Who among us?) Flashes of insight come, but nothing sticks; the poems will not yield to her. As the deadline approaches, we get an intimate glimpse of a mind both at work and at war. Watching Annabel try to push her intellect past new limits may compel a reader to do the same—or perhaps just to read the novel with the same close attention she pays the sonnets. As for whether she finishes her essay on time, I’ll disclose no spoilers here. Guilty Pleasures , by Arielle Zibrak The smutty hockey romance Heated Rivalry is passionately beloved, yet many of its fans admit to being embarrassed by their obsession with the TV series and novels that inspired it. (Ardent and committed lovers of other things—such as, say, hockey teams—tend not to feel the same way.) But Zibrak, an English professor at the University of Wyoming, insists that no novel, film, or show is more shameful, or less worth consuming, than any other is—and that even art dismissed as lowbrow has “much to tell us about ourselves and the world.” In this short, snappy tract, she confidently surveys the landscape of “guilty pleasures”—usually those written by, about, or for women—and unearths newfound complexity. She manages to cover the obscure 1850 best seller The Wide, Wide World as well as Judy Blume’s Are You There God? It’s Me, Margaret , along with critical essays from thinkers such as Hilton Als and Saidiya Hartman; each volume mentioned is worth tracking down. So are other volumes in the series this belongs to, NYU Press’s Avidly Reads. [ Listen: A writer learns how to read again ]

items.title: Zondoma/Tougo : Des orpailleurs offrent des vivres et une enveloppe de 100 mille à la gendarmerie
items.description: Burkina/Zondoma-Don-Gendarmerie Zondoma/Tougo : Des orpailleurs offrent des vivres et une enveloppe de 100 mille à la gendarmerie Tougo, 25 août 2026 (AIB) – Un groupe d’orpailleurs a remis, mardi 25 août 2026, un don d’une valeur de 200 000 francs CFA à la brigade de gendarmerie de Tougo, dans la province du Zondoma. Le don est constitué de quatre sacs de riz de 50 kg et d’une enveloppe de 100 000 francs CFA. Président de la délégation spéciale (PDS), Boureima Souley, cette initiative des donateurs est sans conteste une manifestation de patriotisme qui mérite d’être salué à sa juste valeur. Elle s’inscrit selon lui, dans la logique des orientations des plus hautes autorités du pays, qui invitent chaque citoyen à contribuer dans les limites de ses moyens, au développement du Burkina Faso. « Chacun, en fonction de ses moyens, doit pouvoir apporter sa contribution au développement de notre pays », a-t-il relevé En recevant le don, le chef de brigade adjoint de la gendarmerie de Tougo, Adama Coulibaly, a traduit ses remerciements aux donateurs tout en formulant des vœux de prospérité à leur endroit. « Nous remercions les donateurs pour ce geste. Nous prions pour que leurs affaires se fructifient afin qu’ils puissent davantage soutenir les services administratifs », a-t-il déclaré. « C’est une entrée en matière. Nous allons toujours soutenir la gendarmerie si nos moyens nous le permettent », a rassuré le représentant des donateurs, Idrissa Ouédraogo pour qui cette contribution constitue une première étape. En rappel la brigade de Tougo avait également reçu le 7 août dernier, un kit de matériel informatique et une somme d’argent de la part d’un orpailleur de la localité. Agence d’information du Burkina YN/AK-DNK

items.title: Pourquoi Boubacar Yacine Diallo réclame les comptes de la subvention 2025 aux médias ?
items.description: À travers une correspondance officielle adressée récemment aux responsables des associations de presse guinéennes, la Haute Autorité de la Communication (HAC) a exigé la transmission d’un rapport financier détaillé justifiant l'utilisation de la subvention accordée par l'État aux médias au titre de l'exercice 2025. ​Alors que cette demande a suscité diverses interrogations, le président de la HAC, Boubacar Yacine Diallo, a récemment apporté des éclaircissements sur la démarche de l'institution de régulation. C'était à l'occasion d'une conférence de presse organisée vendredi 27 août 2026. ​Une règle imposée par le Ministère des Finances ​La première raison invoquée par le président de la HAC réside dans le respect de la réglementation budgétaire de l'État. Ce n'est pas une initiative unilatérale de l'organe de régulation, mais une contrainte administrative gouvernementale : ​« […] Ce que le Ministère des Finances exige depuis 2025, c'est que pour payer la subvention suivante, il faut justifier l'exécution de la subvention en cours. […] C'est une décision du Ministère des Finances. Donc, c'est dans ce cadre que nous avons demandé aux associations, de nous produire un rapport financier. » ​Boubacar Yacine Diallo précise que cette démarche s'inscrit dans un cadre plus large de réformes des finances publiques en Guinée. Si la souplesse prévalait autrefois, les standards de gestion ont évolué : ​« Par le passé, il n'y avait pas cette exigence. Mais la Guinée se modernise. La Guinée modernise aussi son modèle de gestion des finances publiques. » ​Le motif central de la HAC est d'anticiper les procédures administratives afin que la subvention de l'année à venir ne subisse aucun blocage. Le rapport exigé servira de pièce justificative indispensable au dossier transmis au Trésor public : ​« Mais ce rapport financier n'est destiné qu'au ministère des Finances et il doit accompagner la demande pour la nouvelle subvention. C'est le seul objectif. […] C'est pour que ce rapport soit fait et que la subvention 2026 vous soit octroyée. » ​Pour mener à bien cette démarche, la HAC met d'ailleurs son propre pôle financier à la disposition des faîtières de presse pour les assister dans la rédaction de ces bilans, évitant ainsi les retards d'exécution constatés par le passé. ​Soucieux de rassurer les professionnels des médias, Boubacar Yacine Diallo a tenu à cadrer strictement le rôle de la HAC. L'institution ne cherche pas à se substituer aux organes d'inspection ou à la justice : ​« Nous ne sommes pas un corps de contrôle de l'État, nous ne sommes pas un démembrement de la justice. Nous sommes une institution de régulation et notre rôle, c'est d'aider la presse à avoir son argent. Donc il n'y a pas de corps de contrôle, il n'y a pas de justice. » ​Il est important de préciser selon la HAC, que la réclamation des rapports financiers de la subvention 2025 s'impose comme une formalité administrative préalable et obligatoire, visant avant tout à sécuriser et accélérer le déblocage des fonds d'aide publique, destinés aux médias, pour l'exercice 2026.

items.title: Zondoma : La jeunesse appelée à renforcer son engagement dans la construction d’un espace confédéral souverain
items.description: Burkina/Zondoma-Journée-Jeunesse Zondoma : La jeunesse appelée à renforcer son engagement dans la construction d'un espace confédéral souverain Gourcy, 28 août 2026 (AIB) – La direction provinciale des sports, de la jeunesse et de l’emploi du Zondoma a commémoré en différé, la Journée internationale de la Jeunesse (JIJ), le vendredi 28 août 2026, à Gourcy. Un panel et une séance d’aérobic ont ponctué cette célébration placée sous le thème : « Rôle, responsabilité et engagement de la jeunesse burkinabè dans la construction d’un espace confédéral souverain ». A l’instar des autres localités du Burkina, c'est au tour de la cité de Naaba Yadega d’accueillir, le vendredi 28 août 2026, la commémoration de la Journée Internationale de Jeunesse (JIJ). Cette activité organisée par la direction provinciale des sports, de la jeunesse et de l’emploi du Zondoma a pour objectif, d’une part, de magnifier une jeunesse résiliente et d’autre part de servir de cadre d’échanges et de sensibilisation des jeunes sur leurs rôles et leurs responsabilités dans la construction d’un espace confédéral souverain. Présidée par le haut-commissaire de la province du Zondoma, Aboubacar Sidiki Nabé, elle a réuni les autorités administratives et coutumières ainsi que des jeunes des différentes communes de la province autour d’une série de communications portant notamment sur l’idéal révolutionnaire, le civisme, le patriotisme et la responsabilité de la jeunesse. C’est le Chef de Bascorma, Naaba Piiga qui a ouvert les échanges en partageant sa riche expérience sur l’idéal révolutionnaire. Il a notamment mis l’accent sur les valeurs et les enseignements que la jeunesse peut tirer de l’engagement des générations précédentes. A sa suite, le conseiller spécial chargé de la jeunesse à la Présidence du Faso, Alouna Traoré, a entretenu les participants sur la vie d’un révolutionnaire, permettant aux jeunes de mieux appréhender les réalités liées à l’engagement révolutionnaire. A son tour, le cinéaste Rasmane Ouédraogo dit ‘’Raso’’ a développé une communication sur le patriotisme et le civisme, avant d’aborder le rôle et la responsabilité des jeunes dans la consolidation de la révolution. « La jeunesse doit prendre pleinement conscience de sa responsabilité et traduire son engagement par des actions concrètes au service de la communauté et de la nation », a indiqué le haut-commissaire qui par ailleurs a vivement recommandé aux jeunes de faire de leur engagement un levier d’actions au service de la communauté et du pays. Les échanges ont ainsi permis de rappeler la nécessité pour la jeunesse de s’impliquer davantage dans la vie de la nation, à travers le civisme, le patriotisme, la cohésion sociale et la participation aux actions de développement. En plus du panel, la journée s’est poursuivie par une séance d’aérobic, offrant aux participants un moment de détente et de cohésion après les communications. Agence d’information du Burkina YN/AK-DNK

items.title: Disciplinary proceedings initiated against 3 cops over alleged involvement in Karachi DHA residents' scuffle: DIG
items.description: KARACHI: Disciplinary proceedings were initiated on Sunday against three cops for their alleged involvement in a recent scuffle between two apartment residents in Defence Housing Authority’s (DHA) Phase 6, a police officer said. The development comes after the CCTV footage of the incident , which took place on August 21, went viral on social media. South Deputy Inspector General (DIG) Syed Asad Raza told Dawn that formal proceedings have been initiated in the matter and the policemen allegedly involved in the incident have been identified. The three were directed to appear before the South DIG tomorrow (Monday) at his office for disciplinary proceedings. DIG Raza also told Dawn that both parties have been asked to attend the inquiry proceedings. Additionally, neighbours were also asked to provide information about the incident and relevant digital evidence. Earlier in the day, Karachi Additional Inspector General (AIG) Azad Khan had sought a report within three days on the scuffle and the alleged involvement and “misconduct” of police personnel in the matter. AIG Khan ordered a “complete and unbiased” inquiry into the incident, instructing the South deputy inspector general to submit a report within three days, an official police statement said. He sought a “fact-based report” on the alleged misconduct of police personnel in the matter, it added. The AIG directed that all aspects of the case should be assessed and those involved should be identified, according to the statement. On Saturday, DIG Raza had told Dawn that he had directed the investigation officer to conduct a probe on merit and in an impartial manner. CCTV and FIR In the CCTV footage of the incident, a woman can be seen rushing down a flight of stairs with a dumbbell in her hand and charging at another woman before using it to hit her. The video also showed two individuals in what appeared to be police uniforms restraining the woman being assaulted, and a man who came up the stairs shortly after and began arguing with the woman with the dumbbell. At one point, the man and woman being assaulted managed to go inside what appeared to be their home, following which the woman with a dumbbell and another man began banging on their door and yelling obscenities. At the end, a man in a shalwar kameez can be seen using a weapon, provided by one of the people in uniform, to smash the CCTV camera. But the incident’s first information report (FIR) offered a different version of events. It was registered at Darakhshan police station at 1:40am on Aug 21 on the complaint of a woman. The FIR seen by Dawn invoked Sections 354 (assault or criminal force to woman with intent to outrage her modesty), 504 (intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of the peace), 506 (criminal intimidation), 337A(i) (punishment of shajjah ), 382 (theft after preparation made for causing death, hurt or restraint to commit theft) and 34 of the Pakistan Penal Code. However, DIG Raza said that Section 382 pertaining to the alleged theft of gold ornaments had been removed from the FIR as the incident appeared to be a case of assault. In the complaint, the woman described herself as a resident of the fourth floor of an apartment building, adding that a man, his sister and their mother — who resided on the third floor — came to their door and started kicking it. The complainant alleged that the three family members hurled verbal abuses over a parking issue, and upon opening the door, began beating and threatening her. Subsequently, local police arrived on the spot and took the brother and sister into custody on the complainant’s statement, while their mother fled, the FIR said. In the FIR, the woman also claimed that the other side “snatched” her gold earring and two rings.

items.title: Burkina : Djibo et Kiembara, théâtres de deux offensives aériennes décisives contre les terroristes
items.description: Portées par une coordination sans faille entre unités au sol et vecteurs aériens, les Forces combattantes ont déjoué début août deux tentatives d’infiltration d’envergure à Djibo et Kiembara, tout en multipliant durant le mois, sur d’autres fronts, les accrochages victorieux face à des terroristes en perte de vitesse. Avec l’installation de la saison des pluies, les Forces du mal pensent être à l’abris grâce à la végétation abondante dans certains théâtres de combat. C’est sans compter sur la vigilance des guetteurs et la détermination des boys d’aller chercher l’ennemi jusqu’à ces derniers retranchements. Ainsi le lundi 24 août, le groupe d’intervention spécial du 23ᵉ BIR a pris contact avec un ennemi dans la zone de Bangossogo. Des dizaines de criminels ont été neutralisés et du matériel récupéré. Cette journée s’inscrivait dans le prolongement direct du 20 août, particulièrement actif. Dans la zone de Welguimsifou, le groupe d’intervention spécial du 30ᵉ BIR a pris en embuscade des criminels, qui avaient fui en abandonnant leur logistique. Le même jour, les hommes du 18ᵉ BIR ont maté des criminels à Gama, tandis que le 28ᵉ BIR, en reconnaissance offensive à Arbinda, a lui aussi pris contact avec un ennemi qui a préféré fuir rapidement. Sur l’axe de Gorom-Gorom également, le 9ᵉ BIR avait fait une brève rencontre avec l’ennemi, confirmant l’intensité des contacts sur plusieurs fronts ce jour-là. Deux jours plus tôt, le 18 août, l’unité fantôme avait déjà conduit une infiltration dans la zone de Bokou, au cours de laquelle plusieurs criminels ont été neutralisés et du matériel récupéré. Le 17 août, les unités du 9ᵉ BIR, en reconnaissance dans la zone de Samboye, a enclenché les hostilités contre un groupe de criminels. Deux jours auparavant, le 15 août, le groupe d’intervention spécial du 30ᵉ BIR avait surpris une bande de criminels, toujours dans la zone de Welguimsifou. Cette unité y a d’ailleurs déjà été à l’œuvre quelques jours plus tôt, le 11 août, tendant une première embuscade à des criminels dans la zone de Koogo voisine. Le 10 août, dans la région des Bankui, précisément dans la zone du Groupement de forces pour la sécurisation de la Boucle du Mouhoun (GFSBM), des criminels venus du nord en grand nombre pour s’attaquer à la localité de Kiembara ont été décelés par les Forces combattantes, qui avaient aussitôt alerté les vecteurs aériens. Une fois les assaillants installés dans une forêt touffue au nord du village, une opération aérienne est planifiée et plusieurs frappes se sont abattues sur eux. Le lendemain, les unités du 23ᵉ BIR et du détachement de Gomboro, accompagnées des VDP, ont procédé au ratissage des lieux pour récupérer le matériel ennemi encore utilisable. La veille de cette opération, le 9 août, une unité du 27ᵉ BIR a mené, à Diapaga, un assaut violent sur une position terroriste préalablement détectée. Au bilan, plusieurs dizaines de criminels ont été neutralisés et du matériel récupéré. Le 7 août, à Gomboro, les boys ont décelé des criminels s’approchant de leur position et ont réagi promptement, en neutralisant plusieurs. Le 5 août a été une journée décisive pour les patriotes en mission dans la région du Soum, plus précisément dans la zone du Groupement de forces pour la sécurisation du Sahel (GFSS). Des criminels venus en nombre important ont tenté de percer le dispositif à Djibo pour attaquer des postes avancés. Ils seront littéralement frappés, avant que les vecteurs aériens, alertés, ne les foudroient efficacement. Les rescapés ayant pris la fuite ont été rattrapés puis traités. Les Forces combattantes sur place vont récupérer le matériel ennemi encore utilisable. Tout avait commencé trois jours plus tôt, lorsque le groupe d’intervention rapide de la même unité avait pris contact avec un ennemi, ouvrant ainsi la voie à cette série d’offensives qui allait se poursuivre durant tout le mois. Sous le leadership du Commandant en chef des Armées, le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, les opérations se poursuivent sur l’ensemble des théâtres pour consolider les acquis et garantir la sécurité des populations. Source : Agence d’information du Burkina

items.title: At least eight die, 18 missing after ferry capsizes off North Cyprus
items.description: NICOSIA, Aug 30 (Reuters) - At least eight people died and 18 were missing after a ferry carrying around 270 passengers and crew capsized off North Cyprus on Sunday, leaving survivors clinging to its overturned hull. The privately owned ferry left the port of Kyrenia at 12:30 p.m. local time (0930 GMT) and immediately started taking on water for an unknown reason, authorities said. It was heading for the Turkish port of Tasucu in the eastern Mediterranean.

items.title: Na Astou Fall invite à une meilleure préparation au mariage
items.description: L’auteur du livre le mariage : ce que l’on ne nous dit pas, Na Astou Fall, a tenté de dévoiler la face cachée du mariage que les parents ne parlent pas à leurs enfants. Elle a invité la population à préparer davantage la jeunesse à la vie conjugale pour lutter contre les multiples cas de divorces. BAMBEY – Présenté au public samedi 29 août 2026 à Bambey, l’ouvrage : le mariage ce que l’on ne nous dit pas de Na Astou Fall a pour objectif d’attirer l’attention de la jeunesse sur les aspects émotionnelle, relationnelle et humaine de la vie en couple. L’auteure, Na Astou Fall, a écrit ce livre de 114 divisé en 10 chapitres pour évoquer les réalités de la vie à deux que vivent les époux dans les couples et que les parents ne parlent pas souvent à leurs enfants. Selon lui, le mariage ne doit pas être un sujet tabou. « Les parents doivent parler plus du mariage mais pas seulement des droits, des devoirs et obligations. Il y a d’autres aspects plus importants que l’on n’oublie. Il s’agit de la patience, de la responsabilité, l’aspect émotionnelle, l’aspect relationnelle entre autres. », a-t-elle dit. Lire aussi: Avec son premier livre, Na Astou Fall lève le voile sur les non-dits du mariage La cheffe de produits informatique considère son premier livre comme une réflexion qui invite les hommes, les femmes, les célibataires pour leur dire que l’amour qui fonde la phase de l’avant mariage (souvent prometteuse) ne suffit pas pour construire une vie en coupe solide. La scientifique a aussi insisté sur le début du mariage qu’elle définit comme un moment de transition, une période de bonheur intense, d’affection vers un apprentissage dans le long terme. Elle a l’attiré l’attention de ses lecteurs sur les péripéties qui testent le mariage à travers les difficultés financières, les déficits de communication avec des silences énervants, les délusions, les attentes, la patience etc. « Ce sont ces problèmes qui constituent la réalité que les peuples vivent au quotidien. Le mariage est une aventure qui mérite que l’on s’y prépare davantage. Cette préparation ne concerne pas uniquement pas seulement l’aspect matériel. Elle touche aussi le travail sur soi, la foi, les mauvaises interprétations des autres, la nécessité d’une créativité, l’obligation d’être patient et une maturité émotionnelle », a remarqué l’informaticienne devant la presse. Oumar Bayo BA ( correspondant )

items.title: A Society of Cheats
items.description: R ecently, I have taken to telling friends that whenever I’m on campus, I feel like I’m trapped in the middle of a crime spree. I’m not talking about an epidemic of overdue library books or out-of-control parties. I’m talking about AI and the ways in which students are constantly using it to cheat on any work that is assigned to them. For those of us in higher ed—and I’ve taught at universities for more than 20 years—such widespread cheating is a baffling predicament. Universities are medieval creations. They are encrusted with eccentric customs, antique bureaucracies, and hierarchical privileges; any significant change typically comes about at a glacial pace. Not too long ago, I was still filling out grades in triplicate. I can liken the arrival of AI only to what it might have been like had a tribe of Neanderthals discovered a flying saucer hovering just outside their cave. To say that we were unprepared doesn’t begin to describe the experience. By now, there have been many articles about how undergraduates’ promiscuous use of AI will affect their intellectual development, but I’m far more interested in its moral consequences. This is partly because I’m pretty confident about the former—I’ve told graduate students who actually learned how to write papers in college that I anticipate a generation of incompetents roughly a decade behind them—but also because I teach classes in leadership and business ethics, and I’m aghast at so many young people seemingly habituating themselves to cheating as a way of life. Many students would no doubt object to this claim, but plainly that’s what they’re doing, cheating their way through their education. Every paper they don’t write, every problem set they don’t prepare, every serious reading they summarize into a memo—all of these are exercises in cutting corners, in getting by, and, at graduation time, in gaining a degree they didn’t earn. [ Rose Horowitch: How AI killed a 133-year-old Princeton tradition ] That word is key: earn . To say that someone “earned” something is to apply a moral distinction to what one acquires. Not only can we get things we didn’t earn, but we can also obtain things we don’t deserve. The first is the good fortune of the trust-fund kid, the second the province of a thief. Students are spending a lot of time learning to be thieves nowadays, and once they receive their dubious diplomas, they will enter the “real world” with all the qualities of a criminal syndicate: a knack for cutting corners, a disdain for community rules, and an assumption that a spirit of integrity, and the sacrifices it assumes, is the reserve of suckers and wimps. We will be a society of cheats. I began to notice the change in the winter of 2023, when some of the writing assignments for my classes at Harvard and the University of Chicago took on qualities I had never seen before: squeaky-clean grammar, a superabundance of bullet points, and fairly robotic reiteration of facts rather than the pleasing lurch of original thinking. This is the horrid house style of AI-generated papers; initially, it was not only the clumsiness of these papers that made them easy to dismiss but also the fact that the students submitting them were outliers. No longer. A spring survey by The Harvard Crimson found that one-third of the graduating class admitted to “using AI for an assignment against instructor permission,” which is a fairly sanitized way of saying “using AI to cheat.” That survey was of students who’d entered college in the fall of 2022, before the mass adoption of AI tools. When it comes to students who are just arriving on campus this semester, I keep thinking about a colleague who teaches freshman composition at the University of Chicago. In the spring, he told me that, across all of the sections he had led over the past year, he believed that only three of his students submitted assignments written without the help of AI. Three students. In a class whose explicit aim is to teach writing. At least part of the reason for this pervasive use of AI appears to be well-founded confidence that cheaters will not get caught, and that if they do, the consequences will be minimal. Take, again, the Harvard survey I mentioned. Among those 2026 graduates who admitted to “using AI for an assignment against instructor permission,” 93 percent of them said their cheating went undiscovered. Of the remaining students, more than half of them said they faced no disciplinary consequences even after they were caught. Just 2.6 percent of these students who used AI “against instructor permission” said they paid any price for their offenses—which, on the whole, is pretty good odds for anyone who is tempted to cheat. For those inclined to break the rules, “playing the odds” is hardly an unusual strategy. It’s the corrupt cost-benefit analysis of fare evaders, speeding drivers, and tax cheats. It treats community rules not as common obligations but as opportunities for risk assessment. In the face of some illicit benefit, the question is not one of right and wrong, but of the likelihood of punishment. Such thinking is especially seductive when it comes to “victimless crimes.” We often use that term, a hazardous oxymoron, to describe activities in which any benefits to the offender seem to outweigh any potential injury to others. To would-be offenders, the moral appeal of carrying out such crimes can be quite powerful, especially when the harm in question is remote or uncertain. They know the good they would enjoy, so it seems unjust and even gratuitous that they should deny themselves the reward when no serious harm would come to others. My hunch is that this is how a lot of students see the unsanctioned use of AI. No real damage comes to any other person when they use these tools to write a paper or complete a problem set. At the same time, especially in a world where everyone is doing it— even some of their professors —why should they put themselves at a disadvantage of time, trouble, and professional advancement? Of course, such logic already accepts one kind of harm: a debasement of the academic experience. A recent case out of Brown University provides a bleak illustration. In the spring, Roberto Serrano, an economics professor, decided to change the exam format for one of his classes from in-person to take-home. This was a generous concession on Serrano’s part to the anxiety that many of his students felt about being back in the classroom after the mass shooting on campus in December. How did students respond? Once they heard about the change, enrollment soared. Nearly 90 students signed up for a class that had never had more than 30 before, and the average score on the midterm was 96, with 40 students “achieving” a perfect score. One doesn’t need the training of a tenured economist to know that this result is improbable. As Serrano told Insider Higher Ed , he ran his exam through ChatGPT and got answers similar to those of his unusually impeccable pupils—“kind of correct,” he said, but “with a very convoluted style.” And so, for the final exam, he switched back to an in-person format. Eighteen students immediately dropped the class. Nine students who remained did not take the exam at all. And among those who did, the average score was 48.6, the lowest average for a final exam in the history of his class by nearly 20 points. Serrano was understandably sore. “We cannot afford to have a society in which a significant fraction of our best young minds think that cheating is OK,” he told Inside Higher Ed . “That leads to a declining society, to a failed society.” The specific failure he had in mind is intellectual—“We cannot choose to become idiots”—but the episode encapsulates the kind of moral rot that sets in whenever members of a community stop regarding rules as obligatory. Set aside the offenders. For students in class who actually care about a subject, they know that they are surrounded by peers who are constantly cheating on their coursework. For professors who are excited to communicate new ways of thinking, they have to face a wall of young people who won’t make even the barest effort to understand the subject matter. And for graduate students who are working as teaching assistants, they have to spend hours each semester grading bogus assignments, at the end of which they face the prospect of having to give out a passel of underserved A’s. [ Read: Why the closing of Harvard’s writing center matters ] This is the upshot of the crime spree under way at campuses across the country and around the world. It doesn’t involve the same type of harm as spiking the water supply or setting a building on fire—harm that is immediate, overwhelming, and undeniable—but, in the long term, it’s no less destructive. It entirely corrupts the integrity of an academic community, because learning in a classroom is impossible when everyone knows that the proceedings are ridiculous. G lacial though they may be , universities are starting to respond. As The Atlantic ’s Rose Horowitch reported in the spring , Princeton’s faculty voted to mandate proctors for all in-person examinations. The decision is the most significant change to the university’s famed Honor Code since it was first introduced in 1893, when the young men of Princeton successfully contended that their word alone should be enough to satisfy any concerns about cheating. For more than 130 years, students have had to attest: “I pledge my honor that I have not violated the Honor Code during this examination.” Henceforward, they will still be asked to do so, but it will be merely a formality. The faculty has decided that students simply cannot be trusted. This is how communities tend to respond to crime waves: They beef up law enforcement. Surveillance widens, punishments stiffen, and legal codes expand to police behavior that was formerly restrained by customary norms of honor, decorum, and mutual reciprocity. As the superintendents of their academic communities, faculty find themselves having to prioritize the disciplinary elements of their job. They will spend more time serving as judge, jury, and executioner, even when what they really want to do is what they do best: research and teach. A suboptimal allocation of academic resources may be the least we have to fear from this crisis in higher ed. Even if faculty can curb this wave of cheating—and count me doubtful—it is the result of an unprecedented number of students deciding that they don’t need to follow rules that disadvantage their own success and advancement, regardless of the implications for their peers and the corrosive effects on their community. This is the mindset that young people across the country are graduating with, one less of strident careerism than of soft criminality. Relative to those who came before them, they will know very little, but they will be convinced of the wrong things, that the world will get along just fine without integrity in one’s work, trust in one’s peers, and pride in one’s community. These are all achievements, things you earn individually and together. You cannot steal them, but they can be taken from you—and they are being taken from all of us, faster than we know.

items.title: « Wakh Niominka », là où se rencontrent la mémoire et le fleuve (2/2)
items.description: Historiquement, le « Tourou Mbossé » a toujours été célébré un lundi après-midi, en plein hivernage. Le rituel est traditionnellement effectué à « Wakh Niominka », un lieu situé à proximité du port de Kaolack, près du marché au poisson. KAOLACK – Le « Bar Mbossé » compte plusieurs emplacements dans la ville de Kaolack. On parle notamment de sites sacrés qui abritent aujourd’hui des services comme la Rts Kaolack, la Gouvernance, le Conseil départemental ou encore le Port. Mais le rituel est traditionnellement effectué à « Wakh Niominka », un lieu situé à proximité du port de Kaolack, non loin du marché aux poissons. Le choix de l’eau n’est pas fortuit. Selon les descendants de « Mbossé », elle constitue l’un des éléments fondamentaux de la tradition. Le cérémonial se déroule dans les eaux du Saloum et non simplement sur la terre ferme. Les femmes de la lignée familiale jouent également un rôle central dans son accomplissement. C’est vers 18h passées que débute la cérémonie, pour se terminer au crépuscule, juste avant la tombée de la nuit. « Ce lieu appelé ‘’Wakh Niominka’’ est un berceau du Saloum. C’est ici que le rituel a lieu chaque année et cela ne change pas. Chaque participant au rituel doit être vêtu de blanc. Les rites sont dirigés par une femme, épaulée dans les tâches par des cousins, cousines ou sœurs de la même famille », raconte un membre de la famille. Lire aussi: Un rituel qui défie le temps (1/2) Les offrandes sont ainsi déposées dans les eaux du Saloum. Elles sont constituées notamment de galettes de riz et de lait caillé, auxquels s’ajoutent d’autres éléments dont seule la famille connaît la composition et la nature. Le tout est accompagné de petites calebasses. Celles qui les portent doivent être de petites filles n’ayant pas encore atteint l’âge de la puberté. Ainsi, la prêtresse s’engouffre dans l’eau, accompagnée de quelques membres de la famille chargés de l’épauler. « Après les offrandes, une partie est versée dans la mer et commence la purification dans l’eau avec la prêtresse. Les vœux sont ensuite formulés, puis vient le bain rituel. C’est l’occasion de purifier certaines personnes malades qui viennent de très loin pour assister à cette cérémonie traditionnelle sérère », raconte notre interlocuteur. Après un long rituel, la prêtresse prie pour un bon hivernage, mais aussi pour l’abondance et la prospérité. Selon les témoignages recueillis, durant cet instant solennel, il est possible que le génie se manifeste et apparaît. « Le génie peut apparaître, mais les autres ne le verront pas. Seuls quelques membres de la famille pourront le voir. Le génie est une femme, une présence physique ayant une forme humaine comme vous et moi. Elle n’est pas le varan que l’on voit, mais ce reptile la symbolise. Cette manifestation du génie est réelle, mais secrète », explique l’un des petits-fils de Mbossé. Malgré l’usure du temps, Mbossé Coumba Djiguène continue de jouer un rôle dans la mémoire des Kaolackois. Pour Cheikh Mbacké Sarr, membre de la famille de Mbossé, le « Tourou Mbossé » constitue un important patrimoine culturel de Kaolack. Au-delà de la cérémonie, il s’agit d’un moment de recueillement au cours duquel des prières sont formulées pour la paix, la concorde et la bonne marche du pays. Interrogé sur ceux qui assimilent ce rituel à des pratiques animistes, M. Sarr rappelle que chacun est libre de s’interroger, mais que les personnes qui connaissent l’histoire et la tradition du ‘’Mbossé’’ y restent profondément attachées. « Le Mbossé, c’est notre histoire », affirme-t-il, soulignant que de nombreux participants reviennent chaque année après avoir, selon eux, vu leurs vœux exaucés. Concernant le choix du lundi après-midi pour la célébration, Cheikh Mbacké Sarr rappelle qu’il s’agit d’une tradition respectée depuis longtemps. Toutefois, il estime qu’une évolution est désormais nécessaire. Face à l’ampleur croissante de l’évènement, il propose l’instauration d’une semaine culturelle du ‘’Mbossé’’. Une telle initiative permettrait, selon lui, de mieux valoriser ce patrimoine, d’attirer davantage de visiteurs et de faire profiter toute la région des retombées culturelles et économiques de la manifestation. Par Mamadou THIAM (Correspondant)

items.title: Un rituel qui défie le temps (1/2)
items.description: À travers le « Tourou Mbossé », certains Kaolackois continuent de vénérer la mémoire de Mbossé Coumba Djiguène, figure tutélaire de la ville, incarnée dans la tradition par le varan, appelé « Bar Mbossé ». KAOLACK – Lundi 10 août. Il est 18 heures. La plage de Wakh Niominka est prise d’assaut. Vêtus majoritairement de blanc, ils viennent de plusieurs quartiers de Kaolack, sous bonne escorte policière. C’est le « Tourou Mbossé », un évènement majeur dans l’agenda culturel de la capitale du Saloum. À Rufisque, on parle de la légende « Mame Coumba Lamb ». À Saint-Louis, on évoque « Mame Coumba Bang ». À Kaolack, il y a « Mbossé Coumba Djiguène ». Pour comprendre l’histoire de ce génie tutélaire, il faut remonter dans la mémoire ancienne du Saloum. Selon le récit transmis par les descendants, Mbossé Coumba Djiguène serait issue de la lignée des Ndiégadoum. Son grand-père, un « Lamane » appartenant à l’ancienne aristocratie terrienne sérère, aurait quitté le Baol pour rejoindre le Saloum, où il fut accueilli par Mbégane Ndour, alors roi du Saloum. La tradition raconte que Ndjira, la mère de Mbossé, s’installa à Kaolack, près du bras de mer. C’est dans cet environnement aquatique que grandit Mbossé. Lire aussi: « Wakh Niominka », là où se rencontrent la mémoire et le fleuve (2/2) Le récit lui attribue une capacité à se transformer en varan pour se déplacer dans l’eau, avant de reprendre son apparence humaine lorsqu’elle se rendait au marché. Ainsi naquit l’image de « Bar Mbossé », le varan devenu symbole et génie tutélaire de la ville. Depuis plusieurs années, au cours de la première semaine du mois d’août, un rituel est organisé annuellement par ses descendants. Des offrandes, notamment du lait caillé et des galettes à base de mil, sont faites au profit du génie tutélaire de Kaolack. Des prières sont également formulées en faveur de l’assistance, de la ville et du pays. « Ce rituel est un héritage ancestral qui a connu, au cours des dernières années, une ampleur jamais égalée. C’est un honneur de perpétuer la tradition de nos ancêtres. Nous devons la préserver et la transmettre, avec un seul vœu : que Kaolack et le Sénégal vivent en paix », renseigne la prêtresse Adja Arame Sall, membre de la famille de Mbossé. Un patrimoine féminin Ainsi, dans la capitale du Saloum, le varan ne laisse personne indifférent. Pour ceux qui perpétuent cette tradition, l’animal est associé à Mbossé Coumba Djiguène. Il bénéficie d’une considération particulière dans l’imaginaire local. Cette relation entre l’animal et la mémoire de la cité est si forte que le varan est devenu une véritable représentation symbolique de Kaolack. « La sauvegarde de Mbossé passe d’abord par la connaissance. On ne peut préserver ce que l’on ignore. Il est nécessaire d’éveiller les consciences et de permettre aux jeunes de connaître l’histoire et la culture de leur territoire », préconise Diouma Seck, directrice du Centre culturel régional. L’un des aspects les plus remarquables du « Tourou Mbossé » est la place accordée aux femmes. En effet, la transmission du rituel s’effectue principalement par la lignée féminine. « Ce sont elles qui détiennent le savoir rituel et qui assurent la continuité de la cérémonie », avance un enseignant à la retraite, par ailleurs membre de la famille. À l’en croire, cette particularité donne à la cérémonie une dimension anthropologique intéressante. « Elle montre comment, dans certaines traditions anciennes, les femmes ont été les gardiennes de pans essentiels de la mémoire collective. Derrière le cérémonial se dessine une histoire de transmission familiale où chaque génération reçoit non seulement un rite, mais aussi un récit, des lieux, des interdits et une responsabilité », explique-t-il. Pour les membres de la famille, cette rencontre constitue avant tout un devoir de mémoire. Un héritage qu’ils souhaitent transmettre aux générations futures afin que l’histoire de Mbossé ne disparaisse pas avec les anciens. « C’est un héritage ancestral. Il nous revient, en tant que jeunes, d’y veiller. Demain, nous serons appelés à le transmettre à nos enfants pour qu’à leur tour, ils perpétuent la tradition », explique Pape Meissa Diop, membre de la famille. Venue spécialement de Dakar, cette femme, qui s’active dans le commerce, ne cache pas sa joie de se retrouver au milieu des siens. « Chez moi, c’est un rendez-vous annuel. Il est inconcevable pour moi de rater cet évènement si important dans notre culture. Les anciens ont pleinement joué leur rôle. À nous de prendre la relève pour que Mbossé puisse demeurer éternellement », affirme-t-elle. Comme cette descendante de Mbossé, ils sont nombreux à rallier Kaolack à l’occasion de cette cérémonie. Une pratique jugée animiste À Kaolack, l’histoire de « Mbossé » est intensément vécue par ses descendants et même au-delà. Mais aujourd’hui, la ville s’agrandit, se transforme et se modernise. Les anciennes habitudes commencent à reculer, tandis que les nouvelles générations sont davantage exposées aux influences culturelles venues d’ailleurs. Certains assimilent même le rituel à des pratiques animistes. Mais les descendants interrogés insistent sur leur appartenance à l’islam. Ils présentent cette tradition comme l’expression de leur attachement à leurs ancêtres et à leur histoire. « Je suis musulmane et je suis une disciple de Cheikh Tijjani. Au cours de la cérémonie, nous prions Dieu, nous prions pour la paix et la concorde aussi bien à Kaolack, au Sénégal que dans le monde », rappelle la prêtresse Adja Arame Sall. Cette dimension explique aussi toute la complexité de Mbossé. Le phénomène se situe, en effet, au croisement de la mémoire, de la tradition, de la spiritualité populaire et de l’identité culturelle. Dans un tel registre, la transmission devient le principal défi. Aujourd’hui, le « Tourou Mbossé » figure dans l’agenda culturel de la région de Kaolack. Le Centre culturel régional considère « Mbossé » comme un patrimoine immatériel à sauvegarder et à promouvoir. Une reconnaissance qui ouvre de nouvelles perspectives. « Un peu partout au Sénégal, des totems sont célébrés. C’est le cas à Rufisque, à Saint-Louis ou encore à Fatick. À Kaolack, le ‘’Tourou Mbossé’’ est célébré depuis plusieurs années et cela repose toujours sur une famille. Cela se passe en une journée, avec sans doute des dépenses. Je pense qu’il y a lieu de les encourager avec l’appui des autorités. C’est le plaidoyer que nous devons porter tous. C’est un évènement culturel majeur de la région de Kaolack », ajoute la directrice du Centre culturel régional, Diouma Seck. MAME MODY MBOUP, ENSEIGNANT ET COMMUNICATEUR:« Il faut un Musée et un carnaval du Mbossé » KAOLACK – Enseignant à la retraite, Mame Mody Mboup est un habitué du « Tourou Mbossé ». Chaque année, il retrouve la mythique plage de « Wakh Niominka », avec la même ferveur. « C’est un évènement ancré dans le calendrier culturel de la ville. Il est célébré au cours de l’hivernage. Entre les mois d’août et de septembre, la famille gardienne du Mbossé, avec les populations de la ville, rendre hommage à ce totem », informe-t-il. Il estime que l’heure est venue d’apporter une nouvelle touche à cet évènement culturel qui ne cesse de gagner en ampleur. « Nous devons aller au-delà de cette célébration annuelle. Organisée un jour ouvrable, elle ne permet pas à tous de participer. Un week-end, la plage serait certainement noire de monde. Il faut aussi créer une Maison du Mbossé pour pérenniser cette tradition.», préconise-t-il. À l’en croire, celle-ci pourrait être, en quelque sorte, un musée où seraient conservés tous les secrets, objets et autres éléments liés à ce génie protecteur. « Cela permettrait aux touristes et aux fonctionnaires affectés à Kaolack de découvrir ce que ce totem représente pour la région », explique-t-il. Pour Mame Mody Mboup, les potentialités liées au Mbossé ne sont pas suffisamment exploitées. Il estime que, sur le plan économique, la région gagnerait à rendre l’évènement plus attractif. « Aujourd’hui, ce que le carnaval de Rio apporte au Brésil est énorme. Moi, je reste persuadé que nous pouvons le faire ici, à Kaolack, avec le Mbossé. Ce qui serait bénéfique non seulement pour la ville de Kaolack, mais aussi pour le Sénégal », soutient-il. Toutefois, il souligne que cette ambition ne pourra se concrétiser sans l’implication des autorités. « Pour y parvenir, il faut une bonne organisation et l’accompagnement du ministère de la Culture. Cela permettrait d’élargir l’événement et d’en faire profiter économiquement et financièrement la ville et le pays. », ajoute-t-il. Par Mamadou THIAM (Correspondant)

items.title: Why Are So Many People Listening to a Podcast About Living in a Convent?
items.description: At a convent in Ann Arbor, Michigan, the bell chimes every day at 5 a.m. Then the 40 or so women who live there year-round—Dominican Sisters of Mary, Mother of the Eucharist—head to the chapel. Their day begins with an hour of prayer, followed by Mass. At 7 a.m., they have breakfast together, in complete silence. Many of them head off afterward to teach at nearby Catholic schools—sisters, unlike nuns, are not cloistered—while the novitiates stay behind to study at “the motherhouse,” as they call the convent. On some days, one of the women—Sister Miriam Holzman, who started living there 20 years ago—turns to a new item on her schedule: podcasting. Back in February, Sister Miriam started hosting Dominican Sisters Open Mic , a weekly show in which she and her fellow sisters discuss topics such as scripture, the saints, and day-to-day convent life. Sister Miriam told me that when the podcast started, she hoped it would encourage listeners to “go deeper in their spiritual life, no matter what their background might be”—Catholic or not, religious or not. The show seems to have resonated outside Catholic circles. Clips of the sisters pla ying the ukulel e and describing an Ultimate Frisbee match have gone viral on TikTok. As of late August, their account on the platform has more than 275,000 followers and more than 8 million likes. The podcast has been featured in The New York Times and on the Today show. Listeners seem to be especially drawn to the sisters’ cheerfulness. They laugh frequently and have an easy way of interacting with one another. “Their laughter seems so stress free,” one commenter observed . Another said, “Sisters, I also want that regulated nervous system laugh.” In a post liked by more than 5,000 people, one listener asked, “Why does being a nun seems so fun even though I’m not religious?” Sister Miriam said that the show’s popularity may be connected to the overall trend of people seeking wellness content online. “People are looking for balance, and so are we,” she told me. “We want wellness too.” Their fixed routine—prayer, study, work, fun—minimizes unnecessary distractions. But the sisters aren’t just offering wellness advice or preaching self-optimization. Their search for balance includes trying to become a particular kind of person in body and soul, and noticing traces of transcendence every day. In one podcast episode, Sister Miriam talked about how, when she struggles to focus or when obligations and to-do lists intrude on her mind, her consistent schedule reminds her that in that moment , she is precisely where God wants her to be. “Which is such a gift,” she said. “I don’t need to be planning the rest of my life.” [ Read: The real religious ‘renewal’ happening in Gen Z ] Resisting the pressure to multitask or worry about the future seems to help the sisters prioritize prayer, a pillar of their Dominican order. At midday, the sisters meditate on the essential Christian belief that the all-powerful God took on human form in the person of Jesus Christ. Later in the afternoon, they recite the Liturgy of the Hours, a set of reflections on the Psalms and Gospels. Many of the sisters have said that after years at the convent, these practices spill over into the rest of their life—when they pray for a passerby at the airport, perhaps, or let out a sudden “Come, Holy Spirit” or “Jesus, I trust in you” at difficult points of the day. Prayer, a sister concluded in one episode , “expands your vision of reality.” It has allowed her to notice “the dew on the grass, or the sunrise on the way to work.” As evening approaches, the sisters return to the motherhouse. They pray the rosary and have dinner together as one of them reads aloud from a recent papal address or a biography of a saint. Then out come the Trivial Pursuit boxes and guitars, the bicycles and Frisbees. As with prayer, recreation time together is fixed in their schedule. It’s not optional. The sisters don’t watch TV during it, nor do they scroll on phones. For all the joy that the sisters display on the podcast, they are also open about the sacrifices involved in convent life. They seldom see their families. Their daily lives downplay individuality: Their sleeping quarters, called “cells,” are designed to be interchangeable and are minimally arranged with a bed, a dresser, a table, an image of the Virgin Mary. Adjusting to the 5 a.m. wake-up call can take years. And like all of us, the sisters are prone to stress and worry. [ From the May 2026 issue: Is hurry the great enemy of spiritual life? ] The contentment that the sisters seem to have despite these challenges may be partly explained by the documented benefits of engaging in religious practices. Clay Routledge, a social psychologist who studies sources of meaning in people’s lives, told me that prayer’s “cognitive and motivational power” can make people more attentive. He added, “It focuses your attention on something; it takes you off of these other distractions and worries, and helps you pay attention to what you care about.” In a 2016 study , psychologists at Georgia State University found that prayer motivated very religious students to “invest a greater amount of mental energy in the performance of everyday tasks.” A study from 2012 found that praying for others made participants feel more satisfied about making sacrifices for others—about living, in other words, a less self-oriented life. Starting at 8 p.m., after their evening prayer, the sisters spend the rest of their night in complete silence. Sister Miriam told me that during this time she likes to pray about both the difficulties of the day and the things she’s grateful for. Another sister said that she sometimes walks up a nearby hill, notices the twilight sky, and thinks of her Creator. Then she returns to the motherhouse, ready for the next morning’s bell to chime.

items.title: Roy Cohn Did It First
items.description: The day after Donald Trump won the 2016 election, the conservative political operative Roger Stone was among the lucky few to get through to him on the telephone. The president-elect reminisced about the long-dead friend who had introduced him to Stone: “Wouldn’t Roy love to see this moment? Boy, do we miss him.” “Roy” was Roy Cohn, who became notorious in the early 1950s as chief counsel to Senator Joseph McCarthy and then built a career as a lawyer and fixer for New York City’s rich and powerful. His roster of clients, many of whom doubled as his friends, included Cardinal Francis Spellman, George Steinbrenner, the media mogul Si Newhouse, and a host of famous mafiosi, including “Fat Tony” Salerno and John Gotti. Trump met Cohn in 1973, when the young developer sought advice about a federal lawsuit alleging racial discrimination by his family’s real-estate company. Cohn proposed countersuing the feds for defamation—even though the company had been marking the applications of prospective Black tenants with a large C , for “colored,” and then telling them no apartments were available. The countersuit, for $100 million, failed as a legal tactic—the company settled with the Justice Department, without admitting wrongdoing, after two years of litigation—but it made headlines, which was the real point. Trump and Cohn had the same attitude toward the law: It was not a system of rules, but a way of getting what you wanted. For a generation of liberal Manhattanites, the mere mention of Cohn’s name produced a visceral loathing. They saw him as a self-serving and unprincipled social climber whose crusade against communism had ruined lives. In documentaries , profiles , and the play Angels in America , he has been portrayed as a villain in the vein of Shakespeare’s Richard III, whose monstrousness can be traced back to his own sense of social exclusion. When Cohn contracted AIDS, he kept his illness and his sexuality secret to the end. He died in 1986 insisting that he had liver cancer, even while enrolled in a clinical trial to receive AZT, an early AIDS medication. In American Scoundrel: Roy Cohn’s Dark Journey From Joe McCarthy to Donald Trump , Kai Bird—writing with his wife, Susan Goldmark, whom he credits with contributing significant research—aims to bring Cohn into focus as a progenitor of Trump. Bird’s previous work as a biographer has focused on distinguished statesmen and scientists of the mid-20th century, most notably the left-leaning nuclear physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer, whom he and Martin J. Sherwin wrote about in American Prometheus , the book adapted by Christopher Nolan for the movie Oppenheimer . Cohn, like Trump, had nothing but contempt for the norms and ethos of that mid-century elite. But Bird argues that this hatred was driven less by a coherent politics than by “dishonesty, narcissism, careless cruelty, and vengefulness.” Both men were avatars of the glitzy New York of the ’70s and ’80s, sharing an obsession with sex, a love of celebrity, and a hatred for expertise. Bird quotes the New York Times reporter Sam Roberts on the lessons Trump learned from Cohn: “1. Never settle, never surrender. 2. Counterattack, counter-sue immediately. 3. No matter what happens, no matter how deeply into the muck you get, claim victory and never admit defeat.” (Bird also implies that Cohn may have had a crush on Trump, blond and blue-eyed men being his ideal type.) In Bird’s telling , the parallels between Cohn and Trump begin with their childhoods. Both grew up in New York’s outer boroughs, in families that were prosperous but resentful of those in the real inner circle. Cohn, born in 1927, lived in the Bronx as a young boy, the only child of a loveless marriage. His maternal grandfather, a wealthy banker, founded the Bank of United States, whose clients were primarily Jewish immigrants. Cohn’s father, active in the Bronx Democratic machine, agreed to marry his mother in return for being made a judge, which her father could promise thanks to his political connections. But the family was plagued by a scandal: The bank collapsed in the early years of the Depression, and Cohn’s maternal uncle, who had taken over as its president, was convicted of fraud and sent to prison at Sing Sing. Cohn grew up without many friends; one of his cousins said that he was the kind of kid who would have enjoyed keeping a snake as a pet and feeding it live mice. His social life didn’t improve when the family moved to the Upper East Side in 1935. Few Jews lived in the area then, but the collapse of real-estate prices in the Depression made it possible for the Cohns to get a place on Park Avenue. Cohn was educated at elite private institutions: the Ethical Culture School and then the more traditional and uptight Horace Mann School, followed by Columbia for college and law school. Thanks to his father’s influence, Cohn quickly got a job in the U.S. Attorney’s Office. He was soon working on high-profile cases against alleged Communists, including the writer Dashiell Hammett and the State Department official Alger Hiss. In 1951, Cohn was a key member of the team that prosecuted Julius and Ethel Rosenberg for conspiring to pass atomic secrets to the U.S.S.R. He intimidated Ethel’s brother David Greenglass, who’d worked on the Manhattan Project, into testifying against her. After the Rosenbergs were convicted, Cohn helped press Judge Irving Kaufman to give both of them the death penalty, hoping that Ethel would feel forced to talk. She did not, and the Rosenbergs’ two children were orphaned . [ From the August 2026 issue: Amy Weiss-Meyer on the Rosenberg boys ] Cohn’s ferocious investment in anti-communism, Bird argues, reflected the fears of New York’s “Park Avenue Jews,” who worried that Jewish Americans would be suspected of disloyalty because of Lower East Side radicals like the Rosenbergs. It also made him a natural choice when McCarthy, then at the height of his anti-communist campaign, needed a new chief counsel. Cohn was hired at age 25, beating out Robert F. Kennedy for the job. He advised McCarthy as the senator oversaw more than 110 closed-door hearings and subpoenaed hundreds of people, many of whom lost their job or faced public humiliation. Cohn was especially nasty toward gay men. Hundreds of federal employees were fired not for being Communists but because they were suspected of being gay . Not that the two were entirely separate in his view; Cohn, like many others, believed that homosexuals were prime “prey” for spies. At the same time, he was the target of homophobic rumors himself, especially about his relationship with David Schine, a wealthy, Harvard-educated young man whom Cohn persuaded McCarthy to hire as an unpaid consultant. When Schine was drafted into the Army as the Korean War was ending, Cohn tried to get him excused from basic training. After these efforts were rebuffed, Cohn called the Army’s general counsel and threatened to “teach the Army what it means to go over my head.” A month later, Army representatives were called before McCarthy’s congressional committee for the first time, setting up a confrontation that would eventually lead to McCarthy’s downfall. Bird argues that Cohn’s willingness to say and do anything to get what he wanted—no matter who might suffer along the way—provided a model for Trump’s approach to political life. [ George Packer: The Mafia style in American politics ] Cohn may have entered American political history because of his role in the Red Scare, but American Scoundrel emphasizes the career he went on to build in New York, where he showed an amazing capacity to escape legal repercussions for his misdeeds. Over the course of the 1960s, the liberal U.S. Attorney Robert Morgenthau unsuccessfully brought charges against Cohn for perjury, obstruction of justice, mail and wire fraud, conspiracy to bribe a city official, extortion, and blackmail. Cohn claimed that he was being targeted by Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy , his old rival: “A few people are out to get me,” he declared. During Cohn’s second trial, his attorney suffered a heart attack. Instead of getting a new lawyer, Cohn gave the summation of the case on his own behalf, and when he was acquitted of all charges, he told the press: “Thank God we put juries between the type of tyranny that Morgenthau perpetrates on his enemies!” Cohn could be charismatic. Ayn Rand fawned over him when they met at a party: “You’ve always fascinated me so much and I believe in so much of what you stand for.” Still, he comes off in this book as smarmy and unappealing, a cheat from start to finish. Bird gives us a litany of Cohn’s pettier sins. In the summer of 1968, he invited Cardinal Spellman and the Democratic politician Carmine De Sapio onto his yacht (named Defiance) to discuss judicial nominations, then wrote it off as a business expense. He and Barbara Walters were good friends and he hinted to gossip columnists that they were romantically involved, using her to hide his sexuality. Cohn had a lifelong habit of eating off the plates of his dining companions without asking their permission. He regularly stiffed his creditors. When one hapless small-business man sent him a memo reminding him of a $10,000 debt, Cohn scrawled a characteristic response: “Dear Louie: Fuck you. Roy.” For Cohn, being gay was a private matter—his business, nobody else’s. Drawing on an unpublished memoir by Cohn’s cousin, Bird details sex parties at Cohn’s townhouse on East 68th Street; apparently the house was also used as the set for a pornographic film (Cohn owned two X-rated-movie theaters in New Jersey). He went out regularly to gay establishments, and the gossip columnist Liz Smith wrote that he “owned a number of successful gay bars around Manhattan.” But Cohn remained intensely homophobic in public, telling people that he believed “gays shouldn’t be schoolteachers.” He lobbied against gay-civil-rights legislation for New York City in the 1970s and early ’80s. In 1978, he told an interviewer that anyone “who knows the way my mind works or knows the way I function in active life, would have an awfully hard time reconciling that with any kind of homosexuality.” The playwright Tony Kushner drew on this idea for the famous monologue that his version of Cohn delivers in Angels in America : “Homosexuals are not men who sleep with other men. Homosexuals are men who in fifteen years of trying cannot get a pissant antidiscrimination bill through City Council. Homosexuals are men who know nobody and who nobody knows. Who have zero clout. Does that sound like me?” the Cohn character asks. “No. I have clout. A lot of it.” A merican Scoundrel offers an effective portrait of Cohn’s role in New York society in an era when sleaze and respectability were not clearly delineated. There is a great deal of salacious gossip; readers will learn far more than they ever wanted to know about Cohn’s sexual habits. Yet despite the extent of Bird and Goldmark’s research, the portrayal of Cohn as an unbounded narcissist misses some of what his life might tell us about the right-wing politics of his era. Earlier accounts have been more sensitive to the irony that Cohn was undone by the same political forces he rode to prominence. The repression of the McCarthy era—the frenetic demands for loyalty, patriotism, normalcy—helped bolster the sexual secrecy and homophobia that compounded the devastation of AIDS in its early years, cloaking the disease in fear and shame. What Bird does give us is a new way to think about Cohn, Trump, and the legacy of McCarthyism. Cohn always presented himself as an outsider facing down a hostile, arrogant establishment, a stance that Trump adopted as he moved into politics. But Cohn’s career depended on being an insider, connected to New York’s media empires, real-estate developers, politicians, law firms, and private schools. Looking at the long arc of Cohn’s career shows how much of McCarthyism was about ambition and careerism, rather than ideology. His friends and clients were obsequious to him because they thought he could get them things no one else could: money, divorce settlements, political influence. Cohn’s commitment to his clients kept him in rarified company until the end. In March 1986, Trump threw a bash for Cohn at Mar-a-Lago , inviting guests such as Lee Iacocca of Chrysler and Manhattan Borough President Andrew Stein. Cohn attended, his skin blotchy with sarcoma; afterward, housekeeping staff was instructed to disinfect the silverware with bleach. In late June, a little more than a month before Cohn died, he was disbarred in New York State for offenses including perjury, misappropriation of funds, and coercing a mentally incapacitated client into signing a will that appointed Cohn executor. A blue-chip roster of Cohn’s friends testified in his defense, including William F. Buckley Jr., William Safire, Barbara Walters, and Trump. [ Read: The myth of Trump’s loyalty ] Cohn insisted he didn’t care about being disbarred. Recalcitrant and self-righteous, he always claimed to disregard other people’s opinions of him. He would have responded the same way to the conclusion Bird reaches in American Scoundrel , that he was an “empty vessel” with “no coherent personal philosophy unless you count his shallow mirroring of Ayn Rand’s celebration of unadulterated selfishness.” But he would surely have been bothered by the epitaph that was included on the AIDS Memorial Quilt —especially the last word: ROY COHN. BULLY. COWARD. VICTIM . *Lead-illustration sources: Bettmann / Getty; Carol M. Highsmith / Library of Congress; John P. Kelly / Getty; Fred W. items.title: ‘The lake is our life’: Protecting a shared lifeline in Uganda
items.description: On the shores of Nkondo, in Uganda’s Kikuube district, the day begins before sunrise. Fishers enter the lake to fish, while families around Lake Albert rely on its waters for food, income and daily survival.
